pulls.title: [ty] Fix protocol methods whose receiver is annotated with the protocol
pulls.body:
## Summary

Since #27301, ty rejects valid implementations of a protocol method whose `self` is annotated with the protocol itself:

```py
from typing import Protocol

class HasMethod(Protocol):
    def method(self: "HasMethod", value: int, /) -> object: ...

class Implementation:
    def method(self, value: int) -> None: ...

x: HasMethod = Implementation()  # error[invalid-assignment]
```

A callback protocol with `__call__(self: "Callback", ...)` rejects every callable except a plain function: bound methods, classmethods, lambdas, callable instances and `functools.partial` objects.

Binding the protocol's `method` to the receiver `Implementation` checks `Implementation` against the receiver annotation `HasMethod`, which needs the same binding again. #27301 made that binding the cached `protocol_apply_self_with_receiver` query, so the cycle is now detected there instead of in the assignability queries, which assume a recursive relation holds. The query's initial value, `CallableType::bottom`, is permissive when it stands for an implementation's method, but it rejects everything when it stands for the protocol's requirement. The fixed point therefore settles on "not assignable".

This seeds the query with the binding that assumes the receiver satisfies its annotation: the same `Self` substitution, without receiver constraints. That matches how the assignability queries treat recursive relations: the relation holds unless another part of the comparison fails.

Closes astral-sh/ty#4746

#27227 and #28671 also change how explicit receivers are bound in protocol comparisons and edit the same functions.

## Test Plan

Added mdtests for a class implementing a method with a protocol-typed receiver, for callback protocols (bound method, classmethod, lambda, callable instance, `partial`, and an incompatible function), and for a specialized generic receiver. They fail on `main` and pass with this change. The existing `ty_python_semantic` and `ty` tests pass unchanged.

## Summary
- `TID251` detects uses of APIs banned by project configuration, including access through import aliases. For example, a project can ban os.path.join with this configuration:

For example, 
``` toml
[lint]
extend-select = ["TID251"]

[lint.flake8-tidy-imports.banned-api]
"os.path.join".msg = "Use pathlib.Path instead."
```
- This example configures only one banned API. For each resolved attribute access, Ruff currently searches the banned API entries until it finds a match or reaches the end. Repeating this search becomes costly when the banned list is large.
- This change looks up the resolved name directly in the existing hash map. It retains the qualified-name comparison and preserves the distinction between implicit builtin access, such as dict.fromkeys, and explicit access through builtins.dict.fromkeys.
- This is intended to preserve existing matching behavior and diagnostic messages.

## Test Plan
- All 29 related tests pass before and after the change.
- Added 12 regression cases covering aliases, exact matching, implicit and explicit builtins, relative imports, shadowed imports, Unicode identifiers, and long qualified names.
- Verified identical stdout, stderr, and exit status across the benchmark workloads.
- Formatting and applicable pre-commit checks pass.
Local benchmark results, using the median of 11 runs per binary in randomized order:

Workload | Before | After | Time reduction
-- | -- | -- | --

Python stdlib, default rules + TID251, 100 banned entries | 639.6 ms | 606.8 ms | 5.1%

pulls.title: [ty] Add compact sets of Salsa IDs
pulls.body:
Add new datatypes for storing sets of salsa IDs compactly.

Salsa IDs are (convertible) into simple integers, and assigned compactly within each salsa database page. This lends itself well to a dense bitset representation. However, the IDs also have a generation number, which is stored in the high-order bits of the `as_bits` representation. Naively, this would cause a bitset's memory requirements to grow substantially once we pass generation 0. So instead of storing a single dense bitset, we store the bitset in chunks, with each chunk storing the offset of its first bit.

We also provide separate types for mutable and immutable bitsets. Immutable sets lend themselves well to salsa interning. They can only be constructed by _freezing_ a mutable set. Borrowed mutable sets can be passed directly to salsa interning constructors with immutable set fields, creating the immutable allocation only when the set is not already interned.

The immutable representation stores all of the chunks concatenated together into a single `u64` slice, and drops consecutive offsets where possible. This lends itself well to being interned. The mutable representation stores each chunk directly, without the consecutive offset pruning, and handles resizing the chunk array as needed as bits are added and removed. It uses the same `SmallVec` optimization as the constraint set's `Support` type, so that small bitsets can be created and mutated without spilling to the heap.

pulls.title: [ty] Compare protocol receiver restrictions before binding
pulls.body:
Improve compatibility checks for protocol methods with explicit receiver restrictions. When both receivers specialize the same protocol, we can use the variance of the protocol's typevars to prove that the target restriction implies the implementation's restriction. This lets us avoid recursive receiver checks that introduce fresh type variables.

We preserve the existing structural fallback when the variance-based proof cannot establish compatibility.

Pulled this out of #29027; it claws back one of the larger perf regressions from that PR, but is a standalone fix that can be reviewed/merged in isolation.

pulls.title: [ty] Report read-only keys when deleting, popping, or defaulting TypedDict items
pulls.body:
## Summary

```py
from typing_extensions import NotRequired, ReadOnly, TypedDict

class Cache(TypedDict):
    value: NotRequired[ReadOnly[int]]

def _(cache: Cache) -> None:
    del cache["value"]
    cache.pop("value")
    cache.setdefault("value", 0)
```

ty rejects all three operations, which is correct, since read-only items can't be deleted or mutated. The messages gave the wrong reason, though:

```
error[invalid-argument-type]: Cannot delete required key "value" from TypedDict `Cache`
4 |     value: NotRequired[ReadOnly[int]]
  |     `value` declared as required here
  |     Consider making it `NotRequired`
info: Only keys marked as `NotRequired` (or in a TypedDict with `total=False`) can be deleted

error[call-non-callable]: Object of type `Overload[]` is not callable   # pop
error[call-non-callable]: Object of type `Overload[]` is not callable   # setdefault
```

The synthesized `pop`/`setdefault` overloads leave out read-only keys. A `TypedDict` whose only non-required keys are read-only therefore ends up with an empty overload set. The `TypedDict` method special-casing already reports "Cannot pop read-only extra item", but only for undeclared keys. The `del` path treated every declared key that couldn't be deleted as required.

This PR applies the existing read-only `pop`/`setdefault` check to declared keys as well. It also adds a `ReadOnlyKey` delete error kind, which skips the "make it `NotRequired`" hint:

```
error[invalid-argument-type]: Cannot delete read-only key "value" from TypedDict `Cache`
error[invalid-argument-type]: Cannot pop read-only key "value" from TypedDict `Cache`
error[invalid-argument-type]: Cannot set default for read-only key "value" on TypedDict `Cache`
```

A required read-only key still reports "Cannot pop required field" for `pop`, because that check runs first. For `del` it now reports the key as read-only, because suggesting `NotRequired` wouldn't make the deletion valid.

## Test Plan

Added an mdtest to the `ReadOnly` section of `typed_dict.md`. Without the fix, it fails with four mismatched diagnostics. `cargo nextest run -p ty_python_semantic` passes with no snapshot changes.

Fixes UP046 and UP047 auto-fixes producing invalid syntax (`T1: (*constraints)`) when encountering starred TypeVar constraints, correcting it to valid PEP 695 syntax (`T1: *constraints`).

The TypeVarRestriction::Constraint variant always formatted constraints as (int, str). When the original TypeVar used starred syntax (`*constraints`), the fix generated `T1: (*constraints)` which is invalid PEP 695 syntax.

Added a StarredConstraint variant to track starred constraint arguments separately, formatting them as `*expr` without parentheses.

## Summary

Fixes item 9 of #29422.

N801 currently strips only leading underscores before checking whether a class

pulls.title: [pylint] Make the duplicate-bases (PLE0241) fix unsafe
pulls.body:
Fixes #18712

## Summary

The `duplicate-bases` (`PLE0241`) fix removes a duplicate base class. That changes runtime behavior: `class C(int, int): ...` raises `TypeError: duplicate base class int` when executed, but the fixed `class C(int): ...` runs fine. The fix was only marked unsafe when comments were present in the base list, so it was offered as a safe fix in the common case.

This PR marks the fix as always unsafe, so it is only applied with `--unsafe-fixes`. The rule docs are updated to say so.

## Reproduction

```console
$ printf 'class C(int, int): ...\n' > ple0241.py
$ ruff check --isolated --select PLE0241 --fix ple0241.py   # before: applied silently
$ ruff check --isolated --select PLE0241 --fix --unsafe-fixes ple0241.py
```

Before this change, the first command rewrote the file as a safe fix. After this change, the fix is reported as unsafe and is only applied with `--unsafe-fixes`.

## Testing

- Added a `class H(int, int)` case to `crates/ruff_linter/resources/test/fixtures/pylint/duplicate_bases.py`. The `duplicate-bases` snapshot test fails on the unmodified code, because the new case is reported with a safe fix and the snapshot now expects the unsafe-fix note.
- Updated the `duplicate-bases` snapshot to show the unsafe-fix note.
- `cargo test -p ruff_linter --lib`: 2818 passed, 0 failed.
- `cargo clippy -p ruff_linter --all-targets --all-features`: no warnings.
- `cargo fmt -p ruff_linter -- --check`: clean.

pulls.title: [ty] Avoid crashes when negating recursive aliases
pulls.body:
Negating a recursive legacy type alias such as `A: TypeAlias = "list[Not[A] | A]"` could repeatedly expand the alias until ty crashed. Preserve recursive alias identity when constructing negations and simplify an exact static complement pair, so indexing an `A` now reveals `object`.

Closes astral-sh/ty#4728.

Stacked on #29427.

pulls.title: [ty] Reuse completed type operations
pulls.body:
We reuse completed member lookups, comparisons, and transformations within a type analysis. Each result records its recursion dependencies; a cache hit is valid only while those decisions remain unchanged. Nested cycles that leave an answer incomplete prevent reuse.

We cache source declarations, field annotations, instance-member types before specialization, and variance expressions. Transformations can also use shared Salsa caches when they only rewrite stored arguments: for example, replacing `T` with `int` in `list[T]` or in an eagerly stored `Self` bound. Transformations that require expansion or semantic simplification retain the caller's operation and its recursion guards.

We also avoid copying unchanged signatures, MROs, and TypedDict schemas, and settle literal, nominal, and reflexive comparisons before inspecting their contents when stored data determines the answer.

pulls.title: [ty] Avoid panic when negating dynamic type aliases
pulls.body:
ty could panic when an exception handler used a negated alias whose value is gradual, such as `Not[Dynamic]` for `type Dynamic = Any`. Negating aliases now applies the same normalization as other negative intersection elements, so an alias of `Any` simplifies to `Any`. The builder retains unsimplified negative aliases to preserve recursive self-references.

Closes astral-sh/ty#4729.

`PLE0643` (`potential-index-error`) counted every element of a list or tuple literal as one item, including starred elements. pulls.title: [ty] Preserve inference from rejected generic aliases
pulls.body:
We retain useful generic inference when a call passes a runtime generic alias where a class object is required. The call still reports an error, but its result preserves the alias's specialization so later checks remain useful:

```python
class Box[T]:
    def __call__(self, value: T) -> T:
        return value

def instantiate[T](cls: type[T]) -> T: ...

box = instantiate(Box[int])  # Still an invalid argument.
reveal_type(box)  # Box[int], previously Unknown.
box("wrong")  # Still rejected.
```

We preserve this evidence in the inference fallback while retaining the unsatisfiable constraint for the original argument. Type-variable bounds still apply. For rejected overload calls, we use the first overload whose only mismatches are generic aliases passed as class objects; a valid overload always takes precedence.

pulls.title: [ty] Validate conditional class bases independently
pulls.body:
We now report `unsupported-base` when a conditional base chooses between a class object and a generic alias or another object with a valid `__mro_entries__` method:

```python
class Base[T]: ...

def subclass(flag: bool):
    base = Base[int] if flag else Base
    class Child(base): ...
```

Both alternatives are valid bases at runtime, though we cannot yet resolve their combined MRO. We check `__mro_entries__` only on alternatives that are not class objects. Invalid alternatives still produce `invalid-base`, with the explanation identifying the relevant instance type.

pulls.title: [`pylint`] Mark fixes unsafe when deleting comments (`PLR5501`, `PLW0120`)
pulls.body:
Fixes #29395.

Both fixes rewrote the `else:` line and silently dropped any comment after the colon. Following review, the fix no longer tries to move that comment. Instead, PLR5501 and PLW0120 now mark the fix as unsafe when the `else:` line has a comment that would be deleted, the same approach as UP035 (#29413). Without such a comment the fix stays safe. Inline bodies like `else: x = 1  # c` also stay safe, since only `else: ` is removed and the comment belongs to the statement.

Both rules got a "Fix safety" section in their docs. The existing PLW0120 snapshots only gain the unsafe-fix note, because their fixtures use `else:  # [useless-else-on-loop]`. New fixture cases cover the unsafe and safe paths for both rules.

I used an AI assistant while working on this and reviewed the changes myself.

pulls.title: [`pyupgrade`] Mark fix unsafe when deleting comments (`UP035`)
pulls.body:
Fixes #29400.

UP035 rebuilds the whole `from typing import (...)` statement from the names, so any comment inside it, like `# noqa` after the paren or a trailing comment on a member, just disappears. The fix was still marked safe.

I went with making the fix unsafe whenever a comment falls inside the import, using the same `comment_ranges().intersects` check as `timeout_error_alias`. Actually keeping the comments would need tracking them per member, which felt like too much for this. Imports without comments, or with only a comment after the statement, stay safe. I also added a "Fix safety" section to the rule docs.

Added four cases to `UP035.py`, covering both repros from the issue, a partial move with an own-line comment, and a trailing comment after the statement.

Heads up: #28394 touches the same files for a different UP035 case, so one of these will probably need a rebase.

I used an AI assistant while working on this and reviewed the changes myself.

pulls.title: [ty] Avoid stack overflows when converting recursive callables
pulls.body:
Depends on https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29410.

Comparing a constructor against a recursive callable type can repeatedly specialize its return annotation. If callable conversion discards the class or instance that produced the signature, later comparisons see different signatures on each step and can overflow the stack.

Retain the source alongside projected signatures, and use that source when guarding constructor conversion. This lets recursion detection connect signatures produced by successive specializations of the same source. For example:

```python
from typing import Callable

type R = Callable[[], R]

class C[T]:
    def __new__(cls) -> "type[C[list[T]]]":
        return C[list[T]]

recursive: R = C[int]
```

We now report an assignment error for this example instead of overflowing. This recovery remains conservative: retaining the source makes analysis finite, but does not establish every valid recursive callable assignment.

pulls.title: [ty] Keep recursive type expansion within its consuming operation
pulls.body:
## Summary

Expanding a type alias or computing a callable signature can itself start other type operations. For example, specializing an alias can simplify a union, which may compare types and expand another alias. If that nested work reaches the same recursive type before we install a guard, or loses the active guard, it can repeat indefinitely and cause a hang or stack overflow.

[#29409](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29409) gives nested operations shared recursion state through `TypeOperations`. This PR changes how we use that state: the operation inspecting an alias, recursive body, or computed signature installs its guard before expanding it, and keeps the guard active while it works with the result.

For example, the disjointness checker previously expanded an alias before installing the comparison's guard:

```rust
let left_alias_ty = alias.value_type(db);
self.with_recursion_guard(db, left, right, |_| {
    self.check_type_pair(db, left_alias_ty, right)
})
```

We now install the guard before dispatching to the comparison. The following excerpts show the path when `left` is an alias, omitting the surrounding match and `nontrivial_check` wrapper:

```rust
// In `check_type_pair`:
let result = self.with_recursion_guard(db, left, right, |comparison| {
    self.check_type_pair_impl(db, comparison, left, right)
});

// In `check_type_pair_impl`:
comparison.compare_source_alias(db, alias, right)
```

`with_recursion_guard` records the active `(left, right)` pair and provides `comparison`, a borrowed `GuardedDisjointness`. It holds the disjointness checker and an expansion context created inside the guard. `compare_source_alias` uses that context to open the alias, then asks the checker to compare its body with `right`. The original pair remains guarded for both steps. If the same comparison is reached again, we detect the cycle and conservatively avoid concluding that the types are disjoint.

Other consumers use scoped views for the same reason. A view provides operations such as comparing a type or inspecting a signature, but does not let a caller take the raw expanded body or signature and inspect it after the guard has ended. A callback alone would not ensure this: the callback could return the expanded body.

Each operation still decides what a cycle means for its own result. For example, a repeated comparison and a repeated attempt to render a type need different responses. Caching must also account for active guards: a result reached while breaking a cycle can depend on which operations were already in progress, so we only reuse it when those recursion decisions still apply.

The diff is large because expanding types and inspecting signatures happen throughout the checker and IDE. We have to migrate those callers to use the guarded operations, including member lookup, call binding, narrowing, subtype checks, and rendering. Some added lines replace existing code; others implement the views, traversal, and caching needed to keep the guard active. This is more than passing an extra parameter through the existing code.

Direct calls and callable conversion enter the same guarded expansion API for constructors and callable instances. The API chooses the source identity internally, so a caller cannot accidentally guard only the exact specialization and miss a chain such as `C[T].__new__: type[C[list[T]]]` or `C[T].__call__: C[list[T]]`. These chains now produce call errors instead of overflowing the stack. Finite chains through type arguments retain their callable signatures, and exact recursive constructors keep their existing recovery.

To recognize growing type arguments, we inspect declared constructor and descriptor members without invoking them. Descriptor reads become edges in the specialization graph: computing whether a call is recursive no longer has to perform that call first. This also stops recursive `__get__`/`__call__` chains whose type arguments grow on every descriptor access. The graph includes the instance returned by ordinary construction, so it also recognizes cycles that alternate between constructing a class and calling its instance.

The same growth analysis covers ordinary instance and class members. For example, checking `class Node[T]: child: Node[list[T]]` against a recursive protocol must recognize that each `child` access revisits `Node`, even though its exact type arguments never repeat. Following the nominal-instance approach in [#27218](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/27218), we inspect declared and inherited attributes, implicit instance attributes, and accessor annotations. Descriptor reads remain graph edges, so classification does not invoke descriptors. Class objects, subclass types, instances, and callable projections retain distinct identities. Specializations that stabilize and comparisons that descend into finite nested arguments keep their existing behavior.

Recursion identities also account for the structure surrounding a recursive reference. For `type A[T] = list[A[list[T]] | list[A[list[T]]]]`, each expansion produces a different union type even though the same pattern repeats. We retain the union, container, and callable structure in the identity while identifying growing references by their definitions. Ordinary finite arguments remain distinct. The existing comparison guard can then stop the growing sequence instead of waiting for an exact type to repeat.

The migration also reports circular implicit aliases through generic aliases and preserves comparisons where several union alternatives together cover a finite type. Negation retains circular alias references, so invalid definitions such as `type A[T] = T | Not[A[list[T]]]` report an error instead of repeatedly growing their type arguments. Recovery discards intersections with circular operands before checking uses of those aliases.

We also preserve inference-cycle markers when unpacking unfinished tuple aliases. For `type Nested[T] = tuple[T, *Nested[tuple[T]]]`, replacing that marker with `Unknown` hid the cycle and let each inference pass grow the tuple. Retaining the marker lets the existing cycle recovery converge.

Depends on https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29409.

Closes https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4148.

pulls.title: [ty] Share recursion state through TypeOperations
pulls.body:
Depends on https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29408.

Semantic helpers need to retain the recursion state of the operation that called them, including when they inspect types from another file. Passing only `ProgramEnvironment` leaves each helper to decide whether to create or reuse that state.

Introduce `TypeOperations` to carry the database, program environment, and shared recursion context. Migrate semantic helpers and `SemanticModel` to borrow it, and preserve the context when switching program environments. Mapping caches remain local to each transformation.

This change carries the existing recursion state through the call graph. The dependent scoped-expansion change makes body inspection and applied-result caching use that shared state throughout an operation.

pulls.title: [ty] Keep recursive reference substitution structural
pulls.body:
Depends on https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29314.

Binding and unfolding a recursive type should only replace its recursive references. Running semantic substitution while constructing that representation can expand aliases or start comparisons before the consuming operation has installed its recursion guards.

Add a dedicated structural mapper for recursive binders and references. It reconstructs stored type structure without inspecting deferred bodies or simplifying unions through type relations. Semantic substitution continues to use the existing mapping visitor.

pulls.title: [`ruff`] Implement `pandas3-deprecation`
pulls.body:
<!--
Thank you for contributing to Ruff/ty! To help us out with reviewing, please consider the following:

- Does this pull request include a summary of the change? (See below.)
- Does this pull request include a descriptive title? (Please prefix with `[ty]` for ty pull
  requests.)

## Summary

Closes #29212

This adds a new preview rule `pandas3-deprecation` for the pandas APIs that were removed in pandas 3.0. As we discussed in the issue, I only included the Tier 1 items, i.e. things that come through a `pandas` import (similar to `NPY201`). Method calls like `df.applymap` are not included.

The rule checks for:

- removed functions like `pd.value_counts`, `pd.read_gbq` and `pd.arrays.PandasArray`
- removed arguments like `delim_whitespace`, `infer_datetime_format` and `date_parser` in `read_csv`, and `use_nullable_dtypes` in `read_parquet`
- removed values like `errors="ignore"` in `to_datetime` and `"pyarrow_numpy"` in `StringDtype`
- old frequency strings in `date_range` and similar functions (`"M"` -> `"ME"`, `"15T"` -> `"15min"`) and old `Timedelta` units (`"H"` -> `"h"`)

I skipped period functions like `period_range`, because `"M"` is still valid there.

Some of these have fixes. Removing `verbose` / `fastpath` and replacing `delim_whitespace=True` with `sep=r"\s+"` are safe. The others (frequency strings, units, `PandasArray`, `infer_datetime_format`, `use_nullable_dtypes=True`) are marked unsafe, because the new names don't work on older pandas versions. I followed how `NPY201` handles this.

A few things I wasn't sure about:

- I made it a rule without a `PD` code, as the contributing guide says for rules not from the original plugin. I can change this if you prefer a code.
- I used the `Suspicious` category like `NPY201`.
- I added `SME` to `_typos.toml` because it's a real pandas frequency alias.

I used Claude to help me with the code and this description. I went through the changes, checked the items against the pandas 3.0 release notes and ran the tests myself.

## Test Plan

Added mdtests in `crates/ruff_linter/resources/mdtest/ruff/pandas3-deprecation.md` for all the items, the fixes, and some cases that should not be flagged (current APIs, period frequencies, frequencies in variables).

`cargo test`, `cargo clippy` and `prek` pass locally.

pulls.title: [ty] Reject runtime generic aliases where a class is required
pulls.body:
## Summary

We now reject runtime generic aliases where a class object is required:

```python
def requires_class(cls: type) -> None: ...

requires_class(list)       # Accepted.
requires_class(list[int])  # Invalid argument.
isinstance([], list[int])  # Invalid argument.
```

This builds on #29403, which introduced separate representations for these two things (without changing checker behavior).

In this PR, we use the alias's runtime identity in type relations and class-only operations, including `issubclass` and `singledispatch.register`. Aliases remain valid in annotations, constructor calls, and class bases.

Note that we [decided](https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4727#issuecomment-6180773907) to special-case NumPy for now to make this workable in the ecosystem.

## Case analysis

### Conditional class bases in SciPy

SciPy's vendored HiGHS code [chooses between a specialized and an unspecialized `numpy.ndarray`](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/19a262b04562aac08b22412fe5c7b7c11ff6085a/subprojects/highs/highs/highspy/highs.py#L1542) based on the NumPy version, then subclasses the result. A reduced example is:

```python
class Base[T]: ...

def subclass(flag: bool):
    base = Base[int] if flag else Base
    class Child(base): ...
```

Both alternatives are valid class bases. Previously, we emitted an `unsupported-base` warning because we cannot resolve the conditional MRO. This PR changes that warning to an `invalid-base` error: once we distinguish the alias from the class object, we check `__mro_entries__` on the union, which incorrectly requires the ordinary class alternative to provide that method too.

[#29415](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29415) validates each alternative independently and checks `__mro_entries__` only on alternatives that are not class objects. This restores the `unsupported-base` warning; it does not add support for resolving the conditional MRO.

### Inference after rejected calls in Hydra-Zen

Hydra-Zen passes `BuildsFn[int]` to `make_custom_builds_fn`, whose overloads accept a builder instance or a class object. We now reject the alias, as intended, but also lose the inferred specialization of the result. A simpler example is:

```python
from typing import reveal_type

class Box[T]:
    def __call__(self, value: T) -> T:
        return value

def instantiate[T](cls: type[T]) -> T:
    raise NotImplementedError

box = instantiate(Box[int])  # Invalid argument.
reveal_type(box)  # Unknown.
box("wrong")  # No diagnostic.
```

The original call should remain an error, but we can still use the alias's type arguments to check subsequent code. [#29416](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29416) preserves that inference: `box` has type `Box[int]`, and `box("wrong")` produces an error, while `instantiate(Box[int])` remains invalid. This is an error-recovery improvement. For overloaded calls, a valid overload still takes precedence over inference recovered from a rejected one.

Closes https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/116.

pulls.title: [ty] Separate specialized class objects from runtime generic aliases
pulls.body:
## Summary

This PR adds a `Type` variant to distinguish runtime generic aliases from class objects that carry specialization information:

```python
from typing import final

@final
class Box[T]: ...

box = Box[int]()
alias = Box[int]  # Type::GenericAlias
cls = type(box)   # Type::SpecializedClass

isinstance(box, cls)    # True at runtime.
isinstance(box, alias)  # Raises TypeError at runtime.
```

Both `alias` and `cls` carry the specialization `Box[int]` in our type model. But `alias` is an alias object, while `cls` is the actual `Box` class. The `int` on `cls` records static information about the instance it came from; it does not mean Python created a separate class for `Box[int]`.

Previously, we represented both values with `Type::GenericAlias`. We need to distinguish them to reject aliases where Python requires a class, such as the second argument to `isinstance`. (If we instead represent `cls` with `ClassLiteral`, we lose its specialization.)

This PR is entirely behavior-preserving, but paves the way for #29405, which uses it to reject aliases where a class is required.

Other changes reorder equivalent union types in existing diagnostics. The observed narrowing and opt-in-warning limitations are accepted for this sync; no unresolved ecosystem blocker remains. pulls.title: [ty] Avoid narrowing generic calls to singleton or dynamic types
pulls.body:
When inferring a generic call against a union declared type, we currently narrow to the first compatible union member, using the chosen member as type context for the call. However, this narrowing can make significant assumptions about the materialization of dynamic argument types, which may permit a given narrowing under gradual assignability. This PR changes our narrowing logic to be more conservative about narrowing to singleton or dynamic members in particular, which can lead to particularly aggressive results.

Note that this issue becomes more prominent after https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/26680, where even `identity` calls can infer dynamic results based on the declared type, permitting narrowing to a dynamic member more often. On main, this only affects examples involving invariant types, e.g.,
```py
def head_or[T, U](values: list[T], default: U) -> T | U:
    return values[0] if values else default

def _(values: list[Any]):
    # main: None, now: str | None
    result: str | None = reveal_type(head_or(list(values), default=None))
    # main: Any | Literal[0], now: str | Any | Literal[0]
    result: str | Any = reveal_type(head_or(list(values), default=0))
```

pulls.body:
## Summary

We now reject runtime generic aliases where Python requires a class object:

```python
def requires_class(cls: type) -> None: ...

requires_class(list)       # Accepted.
requires_class(list[int])  # Invalid argument.
isinstance([], list[int])  # Invalid argument.
```

We distinguish an alias such as `list[int]` from a class object that carries specialization information. This also corrects `issubclass` and `singledispatch.register` while preserving valid alias uses in annotations, constructors, and base classes. NumPy scalar names whose stubs describe them as aliases remain class objects and retain the type arguments that distinguish scalar widths. Specialized-class narrowing remains unchanged.

The conformance suite pin incorporates https://github.com/python/typing/pull/2368, which removes a fixture that passed an alias where a class was expected.

Depends on #29403.

Closes https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/116.

pulls.title: [ty] Diagnose and narrow generic aliases in runtime checks
pulls.body:
## Summary

NumPy's stubs declare `np.int64` as `signedinteger[_64Bit]`. We now use that specialization to narrow `isinstance()` checks while reporting `invalid-argument-type` for the generic alias:

```python
from typing import reveal_type
import numpy as np

def as_int(value: int | np.int64) -> int:
    if isinstance(value, np.int64):  # invalid-argument-type
        reveal_type(value)  # signedinteger[_64Bit]
        value = int(value)
    return value  # Accepted.
```

We retain the specialization when narrowing both branches so code after the check has useful types even when the error is suppressed. The same behavior applies to `issubclass()`.

Closes https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4727.

pulls.title: [ty] Preserve bound receivers for strict signature checks
pulls.body:
Protocol matching could incorrectly establish strict subtyping when an explicitly annotated receiver was only assignable through gradual types. Preserve the bound receiver and its annotation alongside cached assignability constraints, so eligibility uses the active relation after specialization and freshening.

For example, `Source[Any]` remains assignable to `IntSource`, but it is not a strict subtype: `get` requires a receiver compatible with `Source[int]`.

```python
from typing import Any, Protocol
from ty_extensions import static_assert
from ty_extensions._internal import is_assignable_to, is_subtype_of

class Source[T]:
    def get(self: "Source[int]") -> int:
        return 0

class IntSource(Protocol):
    def get(self) -> int: ...

static_assert(is_assignable_to(Source[Any], IntSource))
static_assert(not is_subtype_of(Source[Any], IntSource))  # previously failed
```

This is a prerequisite to avoid regressions in #28303.


## Ecosystem report

50 changes reflect corrected strict-subtype checks for receiver-restricted NumPy iteration and tuple hashing; Ibis adds 12 duplicate copies of existing errors. The existing deduplication of diagnostics on calls to unions of constructors is confined to deferred downstream constructor calls (in Ibis, metaclass `__call__` → generated `__init__`; custom `__new__` → `__init__` is another route); "normal" union constructor calls don't deduplicate. This deduplication should either be applied more generally, or be removed; either one is out of scope here. [Full ecosystem report](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29396#issuecomment-6202295665) (head `0ace479a7f9a`).

pulls.title: [ty] Retry positional matching for tuple unions
pulls.body:
## Summary

We check tuple-union unpacks one member at a time, preserving each member's length and element types. This lets later positional arguments bind to different parameters depending on the tuple member:

```python
def f(a: int, b: str | float, c: float = 0.0) -> None: ...

def example(args: tuple[int] | tuple[int, str]) -> None:
    f(*args, 1.0)
```

The shorter member places `1.0` at `b`; the longer member places it at `c`. Previously, combining the tuple's element types caused us to report that `a` could receive a string.

We require every combination of tuple members to match. Fixed tuples and trailing homogeneous unpacks use ordinary matching; other members can use the positional search. The retry remains limited to one non-generic signature and at most 256 combinations. If any combination fails, we preserve the original diagnostics.

pulls.title: [ty] Retry positional matching with variadic keyword parameters
pulls.body:
## Summary

We allow positional matching to retry calls to functions with an ordinary `**kwargs` parameter. Explicit keyword arguments can fill named parameters or flow into `**kwargs` while positional unpacks divide the positional parameters between them:

```python
def f(a: int, text: str, b: int, **options: bool) -> None: ...

def example(before: list[int], after: list[int]) -> None:
    f(*before, "text", *after, enabled=True)
```

We still check keyword value types and require mandatory keyword-only arguments. Calls that unpack a mapping with `**mapping` remain outside this retry.

pulls.title: [ty] Retry positional matching with variadic parameters
pulls.body:
## Summary

We now retry positional matching for non-generic calls with an ordinary variadic parameter. An unpack can stop before a later positional argument, and subsequent values can fill `*rest`:

```python
def f(a: int, text: str, *rest: int) -> None: ...

def call(before: list[int], after: list[int]) -> None:
    f(*before, "text", *after)
```

At the variadic parameter, one element-type check covers a whole homogeneous unpack. An incompatible unpack still produces an error even if it could be empty. We retain the existing inference and diagnostics when the retry fails; unpacked tuple and `TypeVarTuple` parameter annotations remain outside the retry.

pulls.title: [ty] Retry positional matching for fixed signatures
pulls.body:
## Summary

We now accept calls with unknown-length positional unpacks when their inferred argument types can fill a fixed, non-generic signature in order:

```python
def f(a: int, text: str, b: int) -> None: ...

def call(before: list[int], after: list[int]) -> None:
    f(*before, "text", *after)
```

When ordinary checking fails, we search for one valid placement and check it with the existing argument matcher and type checker. The search preserves argument order, required tuple elements, defaults, and explicit keyword assignments. If it finds no valid placement, we retain the original diagnostics.

Argument inference is unchanged. The retry applies only to a single non-generic signature with fixed parameters; overloads, constructors, variadic parameters, and keyword or tuple-union unpacks retain their existing behavior. Arguments with unresolved lambda parameters and calls requiring `TypeForm` context also retain ordinary matching.

Closes https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/3649.

pulls.title: [ty] Reject attribute writes through object
pulls.body:
Writes such as `x.__module__ = "custom"` are currently accepted when `x` is typed as `object`. Typeshed annotates this metadata as writable instance attributes, but `object` itself provides no instance attribute storage. Accepting these writes is unsound when subclasses can replace the metadata with read-only properties, as permitted by #29373.

Reject these writes through `object` and arbitrary `Callable` receivers, including through TypeVar bounds and constraints, truthiness narrowing, and `NewType` wrappers. Writes through ordinary subclasses, concrete function objects, and class objects remain valid, and unknown attribute names retain their existing diagnostics.

Follow-up to [the discussion on #29373](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29373#issuecomment-6175211217).

## Ecosystem report

Analyzed [`3947cc37`](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/commit/3947cc372b18faf15b15930f13740cf363b1faa1): metadata writes through receivers without a writable attribute contract produce 50 new diagnostics and one revised diagnostic. More precise sentinel overload selection in scipy-stubs removes 12 incorrect type-assertion diagnostics and corrects deprecation warnings. All ecosystem changes are expected; CI is green and no readiness blockers remain. [Full ecosystem analysis](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29386#issuecomment-6177077279).

pulls.title: [ty] Clarify object attribute write-contract rationale
pulls.body:
Explain why typeshed's metadata annotations on `object` do not impose writable instance contracts on subclasses. Clarify the implementation comment and the slotted-class regression's prose.

Follow-up to #29373.

pulls.title: [ty] Clarify go-to-implementation search prefilters
pulls.body:
## Summary

Previously, the textual pre-filters for go-to-implementation were unclear in two respects:

- The two pre-filters, one for the member name and another for the `class` keyword, were implemented in two different places in the source code
- The `name_matcher` field checked for each file could hold either a matcher for the `class` keyword or a matcher for the member name, which made its behaviour hard to understand at its usage site.

This clarifies the pre-filters by keeping both checks together and by making the `name_matcher` field consistently search for the member name (with the `class` keyword search implemented separately). It also prepares go-to-implementation for #29232, which releases scanned closed files' ASTs to reduce pauses during database updates.

/xref https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/3909

## Test Plan

This is a behaviour-preserving refactor that relies on existing tests.

pulls.title: [ty] Expand tuple-union unpacks across positional matches
pulls.body:
## Summary

We now check each member of an unpacked tuple union separately when its members place later arguments at different parameters, including calls with a single signature:

```python
def f(a: int, b: str, c: str = ""): ...

def call(values: tuple[int] | tuple[int, str]):
    f(*values, "text")
```

Both tuple members produce valid calls: `"text"` fills `b` for the shorter tuple and `c` for the longer one. Previously, combining the tuple's element types lost that distinction and caused us to reject the call.

Every expanded call must succeed; a valid shorter tuple cannot hide an incompatible longer one. We reuse the argument types when checking each member, and generic return types include the result from each member. Expansion uses the existing limit on the number of alternatives.

Alternative matching is limited to scalar literals and references to already-typed values. Context-dependent arguments and constructor calls retain their existing matching, argument expansion, and inference behavior.

pulls.title: [ty] Avoid writable override contracts from object
pulls.body:
Fix false `invalid-mutable-override` diagnostics when slotted classes assign metadata such as `__module__`. The attributes declared on `object` do not establish an instance-write contract for subclasses, because `object` provides no instance attribute storage. Read-type compatibility and write contracts explicitly declared by user-defined bases remain checked.

Fixes astral-sh/ty#4725.

## Test plan

Checked CPython 3.13 behavior: assignments to `__module__`, `__doc__`, `__annotations__`, `__dict__`, and `__str__` on `object()` fail. Also verified that `__class__` assignment fails for `object()` but can succeed between compatible slotted user-defined classes.

## Ecosystem report

Analyzed head: [`56847d246246b4381d4873a36495e0d91d89f469`](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/commit/56847d246246b4381d4873a36495e0d91d89f469). The ecosystem shows 23 expected false-positive removals across eight projects: getter-only metadata properties and metadata assignments in slotted class bodies. All changes are intended, with no ecosystem concerns remaining. [Full report](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29373#issuecomment-6173018962).

pulls.title: [ty] Fix instance layout conflict detection for inherited classes
pulls.body:
<!--
Thank you for contributing to Ruff/ty! To help us out with reviewing, please consider the following:

- Does this pull request include a summary of the change? (See below.)
- Does this pull request include a descriptive title? (Please prefix with `[ty]` for ty pull
  requests.)
- Does this pull request include references to any relevant issues?
- Does this PR follow our AI policy (https://github.com/astral-sh/.github/blob/main/AI_POLICY.md)?
-->

## Summary

astral-sh/ty#4708 이슈로 제기했던 버그를 해결합니다.
'ty' 여러 클래스를 의심할 때 보는 'instance-layout-conflict'에서 특정 관련 구조에서 진단이 발생하지 않는 문제였습니다.
해당 문제는 base class 목록에 충돌(conflict)하는 disjoint base들의 공통 조상이 함께 있으면 instance-layout-conflict가 나지 않았습니다.  
(CPython에서는 이런 class가 정의되는 시점에 TypeError를 냅니다.)

<!-- What's the purpose of the change? What does it do, and why? -->

원인은 `IncompatibleBases::remove_redundant_entries`의 비교 방향이 반대였기 때문입니다.
{object, int, str}이 {object}로 줄어들어 충돌이 가려지는 것(bug의 원인)의 순서를 바꾸었습니다. 
다른 후보의 상위 클래스에 해당하는 후보를 제거하고, 보다 구체적인 하위 클래스 후보를 유지하도록 했습니다.

이 함수는 class문, `type()`, `types.new_class()`가 함께 쓰기 때문에, 이번 수정은 세 가지 경로 모두에 적용됩니다.

## Test Plan

<!-- How was it tested? -->

- mdtest 추가
      - `instance_layout_conflict.md:` 일반 클래스가 앞/뒤에 섞인 경우, 공통 조상을 상속 목록에 직접 나열한 경우
      - `call/type.md`: `type()`로 만든 클래스에서 레이아웃 충돌 
      - `call/new_class.md`: `types.new_class()`로 만든 클래스. 레이아웃 충돌 테스트랑 기본 케이스도 함께 추가
- 수정 전 코드에서는 새로 추가한 부분만 fail하고, 수정 후에는 pass하는 것을 확인
- 조상과 자손을 함께 쓰는 정상 조합(C(B, A), FF(CC, DD), 제네릭 asyncio 예제)은 그대로 pass (기존과 동일)
- `ty_python_semantic` 테스트 전체 통과(mdtest 502개 포함)
- clippy와 prek 통과

---

> ## Summary
> 
> Fixes the bug reported in issue #4708.
> 
> The `instance-layout-conflict` diagnostic in ty was not emitted for certain inheritance structures involving multiple classes.
> 
> Specifically, the diagnostic was not emitted when the base class list included a common ancestor of otherwise incompatible (disjoint) bases. (CPython raises a `TypeError` when such a class is defined.)
> 
> The cause was that the comparison direction in `IncompatibleBases::remove_redundant_entries` was reversed.
> 
> The order of operations that caused the bug, where `{object, int, str}` was reduced to `{object}` and the conflict was masked, has been reversed. Candidates that are superclasses of other candidates are now removed, preserving the more specific subclass candidates.
> 
> Since this function is shared by class statements, `type()`, and `types.new_class()`, this fix applies to all three paths.
> 
> ## Test Plan
> 
> - Added mdtests:
>   - `instance_layout_conflict.md`: Cases where ordinary classes appear before or after the incompatible bases, and cases where a common ancestor is explicitly listed in the base class list.
>   - `call/type.md`: Layout conflicts in classes created with `type()`.
>   - `call/new_class.md`: Classes created with `types.new_class()`. Added both layout conflict tests and basic test cases, as there were no existing layout conflict tests.
> - Verified that only the newly added tests fail with the original code and pass after the fix.
> - Verified that valid combinations involving both ancestors and descendants (`C(B, A)`, `FF(CC, DD)`, and the generic `asyncio` example) still pass, unchanged from before.
> - All `ty_python_semantic` tests passed, including 502 mdtests.
> - Clippy and Prek passed.

pulls.title: Limit Renovate MSRV updates to the root manifest
pulls.body:
Renovate proposes updating the MSRV of the vendored `ruff_unicode_names2_generator` crate, but I believe we deliberately keep the upstream crate's older MSRV here to minimize differences from upstream.

This PR limits the MSRV custom Renovate manager to the root `Cargo.toml`, so it continues to update the workspace MSRV without proposing updates to MSRV pins in nested manifests.

Closes [https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29359](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29359)

pulls.title: Pin Python for py-fuzzer and scripts CI checks
pulls.body:
After [#29364](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29364) upgraded uv to 0.13.1, the [`cargo test (linux)` job on `main`](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/actions/runs/38555989744/job/115825271718) failed. uv 0.13 defaults to downloading Python 3.15 when no version is requested and no compatible interpreter is already installed. In the failing job, `Run tests` used Python 3.15, and the later py-fuzzer dogfooding step failed to install locked MarkupSafe because the pinned version of MarkupSafe doesn't have published wheels for 3.15, but source builds are disabled by py-fuzzer's `pyproject.toml` file:

https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/9ff6b0f0d27dcbac5a1e6447a336ad8562720f3c/python/py-fuzzer/pyproject.toml#L100-L101

In the [corresponding PR job](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/actions/runs/38553508773/job/115817479045), the preceding "annotation mdtests" step ran, and `Run tests` used Python 3.13. The mdtests can install a Python version that uv later reuses, which may explain why the py-fuzzer step passed on the PR. The annotation mdtests are skipped on pushes to `main`.

This PR fixes the issue by setting `PYTHON_VERSION` (currently 3.14) explicitly for py-fuzzer's dogfooding, lint, format, and type checks. We set `UV_PYTHON` for the scripts dogfooding step too, so that both its uv command and the uv subprocesses ty starts for script dependencies use the configured version. This also avoids selecting Python 3.15 for locked script dependencies that lack wheels for it.

pulls.title: Group phf and phf_codegen updates
pulls.body:
## Summary

Ruff uses `phf_codegen` to generate a Unicode alias map and `phf` to look up values in it. The generated map must be compatible with the lookup implementation; updating `phf` alone can make lookups fail. For example, [#29362](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29362) fails Unicode alias tests.

Group Renovate updates to both crates when both are available so they can be reviewed together, following the existing rule for `strum` and `strum_macros`. Renovate can still propose an update to one crate on its own if the other update is unavailable.

pulls.title: [`perflint`] Avoid invalid comprehension suggestions (`PERF401`, `PERF403`)
pulls.body:
Fixes #29365.

When the loop iterable was a ternary (or a lambda), the PERF401/PERF403 fix pasted it into the comprehension as-is, which isn't valid Python, so Ruff rolled the fix back. Now the iterable gets parenthesized in those cases. If the iterable contains a walrus, I just skip the fix and keep the diagnostic, since that can't go in a comprehension iterable even with parens.

Test plan: added the examples from the issue plus ternary, lambda and walrus cases to the PERF401/PERF403 fixtures and updated the snapshots. `cargo test -p ruff_linter perflint` passes, and the repro from the issue now fixes cleanly.

I used Claude to help with this change and reviewed and tested it myself.

### [`v0.13.1`](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#0131)

Released on 2026-10-14.

##### Enhancements

##### Python

##### Preview features

- Allow `uv tool upgrade` to upgrade installed tools when `tool-install-locks` is enabled ([#​22498](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22498))
- Add preliminary support for parsing PEP 825 variant labels in wheel filenames with `wheel-variants` ([#​22039](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22039))

##### Performance

- Reduce uv's binary size ([#​22429](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22429), [#​22430](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22430), [#​22432](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22432))
- Speed up Simple API parsing ([#​22429](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22429))
- Reduce package metadata parsing overhead ([#​22239](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22239))

##### Bug fixes

- Prevent tool and managed Python uninstalls from deleting unrelated files beside their storage directories ([#​22495](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22495))
- Restore support for source distributions containing hard links or full-length tar user or group names ([#​22516](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22516), [#​22522](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22522))
- Preserve device files and FIFOs used as `uv pip compile` or `uv export` output destinations ([#​22496](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22496))
- Fix `sys._base_executable` detection for environments created from symlinked interpreters ([#​22520](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22520))
- Prevent concurrent readers from observing partially written lockfiles, Python version files, or managed Python sysconfig files ([#​22399](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22399), [#​22402](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22402), [#​22403](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22403))
- Serialize concurrent project commands that reach the same environment through real and symlinked paths ([#​22390](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22390))
- Prevent installs, syncs, and environment creation from failing when they race with `uv cache clean` ([#​22387](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22387))
- Prevent concurrent tool installations from corrupting an environment when the last tool is uninstalled ([#​22391](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22391))
- Persist changed upgrade settings even when `uv tool upgrade` leaves the tool version unchanged ([#​22499](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22499))
- Reuse environments with installed Git dependencies pinned to full commit hashes without resolving again ([#​22464](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22464))

##### Documentation

- Explain how to select an emulated Python interpreter on Windows ARM64 when native wheels are unavailable ([#​22424](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22424))
- Fix the `.netrc` format documentation link ([#​22514](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22514))

##### Other changes

- Publish Python 3.15-based uv Docker images under stable tags ([#​22503](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22503))

### [`v0.13.0`](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#0130)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/compare/0.12.24...0.13.0)

Released on 2026-10-09.

uv 0.13.0 makes Python 3.15 the default stable Python version. We've also included several breaking changes to improve correctness, performance, and compatibility, described below.

**We expect most users to be able to upgrade without making changes.**

While not a breaking change, this release also updates the format of many of uv's cache entries to improve performance. **uv may download or rebuild dependencies after upgrading**, because some cached entries from earlier versions cannot be reused. Multiple versions of uv can still safely share the same cache directory.

There are no breaking changes to the configuration of the [uv build backend](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/build-backend/). If your `[build-system]` table includes an upper bound on `uv_build`, update it to allow `uv_build` 0.13, e.g., `uv_build>=0.13.0,<0.14`.

##### Breaking changes

- **Use Python 3.15 as the default stable version**

  The default stable Python version has changed from 3.14 to 3.15. This affects Python downloads when no version is requested or pinned, e.g., when running `uv python install`.

  uv continues to use compatible Python installations that are already present. For example, `uv venv` can still use an installed Python 3.14. If no suitable interpreter is installed and automatic downloads are enabled, commands such as `uv venv` and `uvx python` can now download Python 3.15.

  You can opt out of this behavior by requesting Python 3.14 explicitly, e.g., `uv venv --python 3.14`. For projects, use `uv python pin 3.14` to record the version in `.python-version`.

- **Honor `--require-hashes` in included constraints files** ([#​22275](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22275))

  Previously, uv ignored `--require-hashes` in constraints files included with `-c` from a requirements file. Now, uv honors the directive and requires hashes for all requirements in the installation. Installs that previously succeeded can now fail if a requirement is missing a hash.

  You cannot opt out while the directive is present. Add the missing hashes to your requirements, or remove the `--require-hashes` directive from the included constraints file if hash checking is not intended.

- **Prefer native Python on Windows ARM64** ([#​22100](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22100))

  Previously, ARM64 builds of uv preferred emulated `x86_64` Python installations because native wheel support was limited. Now, uv prefers native ARM64 (`aarch64`) interpreters across Python versions.

  This follows similar changes in [CPython](https://discuss.python.org/t/python-on-windows-arm64/104524), the official Windows [Python install manager](https://discuss.python.org/t/python-install-manager-26-4/108846), and GitHub's [actions/setup-python](https://redirect.github.com/actions/setup-python#supported-architectures).

  When a native interpreter is unavailable, uv continues to fall back to `x86_64`, then 32-bit `x86`.

  You can opt out of this behavior by setting `UV_PYTHON_ARCH=x86_64` or requesting an explicit architecture, e.g., `cpython-3.14-windows-x86_64`. If you are using `setup-uv`, you can set [`python-arch: x86_64`](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/setup-uv#python-architecture) instead.

- **Reject editable requirements in included constraints files** ([#​22282](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22282))

  Previously, uv silently ignored editable (`-e`) requirements in constraints files included with `-c` from a requirements file. Now, uv rejects these requirements with an error, matching [pip's behavior](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/user_guide/#constraints-files).

  You cannot opt out of this behavior. Move editable requirements to a requirements file passed with `-r`, or pass them directly with `--editable`, instead of including them in a constraints file.

- **Omit the distutils startup patch on Python 3.10 and later** ([#​22096](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22096))

  Previously, uv installed `_virtualenv.py` and `_virtualenv.pth` into every new virtual environment to prevent distutils configuration from changing installation paths. Now, like [`virtualenv` 21.6.0](https://redirect.github.com/pypa/virtualenv/releases/tag/21.6.0), uv omits these files on Python 3.10 and later, which already ignore the affected configuration keys. This reduces Python startup overhead. Python 3.9 and earlier retain the patch.

  You cannot opt out of this behavior. Existing virtual environments are not modified automatically. Recreate an environment with Python 3.10 or later to remove the patch.

  This stabilizes the `no-distutils-patch` preview feature.

- **Treat requirement-file option values as single paths** ([#​22290](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22290))

  Previously, uv split values passed to `--constraint`, `--override`, `--exclude`, and `--build-constraint` on spaces, even when quoted. Now, each value is treated as a single path, allowing file paths containing spaces.

  You cannot opt out of this behavior. Repeat the option to provide multiple files. For example, replace `-c "a.txt b.txt"` with `-c a.txt -c b.txt`.

  Space-separated lists in `UV_CONSTRAINT`, `UV_OVERRIDE`, `UV_EXCLUDE`, and `UV_BUILD_CONSTRAINT` remain supported.

- **Use `tar-codec` for tar archives by default** ([#​22094](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22094))

  Previously, uv used `astral-tokio-tar` to extract tar archives, build source distributions with `uv_build`, and read their metadata for `uv publish`. Now, uv uses `tar-codec`, which applies stricter validation when reading archives.

  uv may now reject archives containing hard links or unsupported tar extensions that previous versions accepted. Source distributions created by `uv_build` can also have different archive bytes and hashes.

  You can opt out of this behavior by setting `UV_LEGACY_TAR_BACKEND=1`.

  This stabilizes the `tar-codec` preview feature.

- **Reject `uv build --clear` output directories that contain a build source**
  ([#​22276](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22276))

  Previously, `uv build --clear` could delete a project or input source distribution when the
  output directory contained the source. Now, uv rejects these output directories, including
  equivalent paths reached through symlinks, before clearing any build output.

  Select an output directory that does not contain any build sources, or omit `--clear`.

##### Python

- Add CPython 3.15.0 ([#​22400](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/22400))

##### Preview features

- Require hashes for build dependencies, including transitive dependencies, with `--require-build-hashes` ([#​21411](https://redirect.github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/21411))

### [`v4.131.1`](https://redirect.github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/blob/HEAD/packages/wrangler/CHANGELOG.md#41311)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/compare/wrangler@4.131.0...wrangler@4.131.1)

##### Patch Changes

- [#​15592](https://redirect.github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/pull/15592) [`945aaa3`](https://redirect.github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/commit/945aaa32e0c38116e501f8509884cb1cc8f1d51b) Thanks [@​WillTaylorDev](https://redirect.github.com/WillTaylorDev)! - Add a provisioning delay note when custom domain Preview URLs change

  Wrangler now explains that DNS and TLS certificate provisioning may continue after a deploy adds a custom domain or enables its Preview URLs. Stable redeploys don't repeat the note.

  This assumes that a request which matches the stored custom domain state doesn't restart provisioning. The client infers this from the API changeset and current domain record because this repository can't verify the backend behavior.

- [#​15592](https://redirect.github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/pull/15592) [`945aaa3`](https://redirect.github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/commit/945aaa32e0c38116e501f8509884cb1cc8f1d51b) Thanks [@​WillTaylorDev](https://redirect.github.com/WillTaylorDev)! - Clarify production status labels for custom domain routes

  Wrangler now prefixes explicit custom domain production states with `production:` so they match Preview labels. The updated labels appear in deployed trigger output and `WRANGLER_OUTPUT_FILE_PATH`.

- [#​15602](https://redirect.github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/pull/15602) [`47d906f`](https://redirect.github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/commit/47d906f52d109509f61b1c801c1b08ecad583c0d) Thanks [@​dependabot](https://redirect.github.com/apps/dependabot)! - Update dependencies of "miniflare", "wrangler"

  The following dependency versions have been updated:

  | Dependency                                                               | From          | To            |
  | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------- | ------------- |
  | [@​cloudflare/workers-types](https://redirect.github.com/cloudflare/workers-types) | ^5.20260910.1 | ^5.20260911.1 |
  | workerd                                                                  | 1.20260910.1  | 1.20260911.1  |

- [#​15592](https://redirect.github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/pull/15592) [`945aaa3`](https://redirect.github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/commit/945aaa32e0c38116e501f8509884cb1cc8f1d51b) Thanks [@​WillTaylorDev](https://redirect.github.com/WillTaylorDev)! - Avoid replacement prompts for custom domains already on the Worker

  Wrangler now updates Preview settings without asking to replace a custom domain when that domain already belongs to the deployed Worker. It still asks before replacing domains attached to another Worker.
