Union normalization already checks whether the incoming type equals each existing element. We reuse that result for the two directed redundancy checks.

pulls.title: [ty] Cache nominal redundancy by class
pulls.body:
## Summary

When the target has no type arguments or its own tuple specification, nominal redundancy depends on the classes. Cache that relation directly instead of interning a `TypePair` containing the full instance types.

For static classes, use the two interned class handles as the key. The new queries use the existing relation and cycle initialization.

pulls.title: [`flake8-tidy-imports`] Fix `lazy-import-mismatch` (`TID254`) fix corruption with extra whitespace and `lazy-import-immediately-resolved` (`TID255`) false positives in `for` loops
pulls.body:
## Summary

The `ban-lazy` fix in `lazy-import-mismatch` deleted a hardcoded 5-byte range, assuming `lazy` is followed by exactly one whitespace byte. With extra whitespace (`lazy  import foo`, valid since `lazy` is a soft keyword), the fix left a stray leading space, producing an `IndentationError`. The fix now reuses the token-scanned `lazy_import_prefix_range` from `lazy-import-immediately-resolved`, which deletes from the `lazy` token through the whitespace before `import`/`from`.

`lazy-import-immediately-resolved` treated module-level `for` loop bodies as unconditional: a name used only inside a `for` body was flagged as immediately resolved even though the body may execute zero times. `on_conditional_branch` now includes `For` (sync and async), consistent with `If`/`While`/`Match`. The iterable itself is still flagged since it always evaluates.

## Test Plan

- New `lazy_import_mismatch_ban_lazy_extra_whitespace` test with two-space and tab-separated lazy imports; fails on main (the fixed output retains a leading space), passes with the change.
- The `TID255.py` fixture gains module-level `for` and `while` cases; the snapshot shows the iterable flagged and the loop body unflagged.
- `cargo test -p ruff_linter --lib` passes (2836 tests).

pulls.title: [ty] Defer recursive TypedDict value projections
pulls.body:
## Summary

We avoid stack overflows when constructing the value type of a recursively specialized `TypedDict`. Even a known-key `get` call constructs a fallback overload whose return type includes every possible value:

```python
from typing_extensions import ReadOnly, TypedDict

class Node[T](TypedDict, extra_items=ReadOnly["Node[list[T]]"]):
    value: T

def read(node: Node[int]) -> int:
    return node.get("value")
```

The value projection uses the existing `RecursiveType` representation from #28425. It stores the declaration and type arguments until an operation needs the value union. Constructing or specializing that union avoids redundancy comparisons that could request another projection before the first one finishes.

Unfolding can expose a union that contains the same recursive type again, so the guard covers both unfolding and inspection of the resulting body. Semantic expansion normalizes outer aliases and unions before callers inspect them, using the existing union-expansion machinery to preserve shared recursive alternatives. Queries, stateful walks, and checks that compare two types use the same normalization. This also prevents equality narrowing from exploring every path through a shared recursive graph. Recursive calls retain their guards and mapping visitor; each operation chooses its own cycle result, and comparisons keep both operands in their recursion key.

Queries reuse completed results by type and per-call input, including descriptor receivers. The cache checks local guard dependencies before reusing an answer and discards cached answers when the shared guard context changes. This prevents partial answers from escaping the cycle in which they were computed. Stateful walks use the same normalization without caching their callbacks. Attribute-deletion checks return an error for the caller to report after the query, so reusing a result does not suppress a diagnostic.

Raw unfolding is private. Structural transformations use a separate traversal mode and expansion context to retain the original alternatives. Union construction, parameter collection, and dependency analysis need those original edges because normalization can remove a redundant alternative that still contains a relevant parameter. Pydantic's lax input conversion also preserves alias boundaries while descending into container arguments, so its recursion guards remain effective. Semantic expansion contexts cannot expose an unnormalized recursive body.

Inspections retain whether normalization passed through a union. Contextual inference and union filtering can therefore use a union that collapses to one alternative without changing how they handle an ordinary alias.

Attribute writes keep union and intersection requirements deferred. Assignment inference, protocol compatibility, and deprecation checks consume them under the same guard, so shared recursive types stay shared.

Union expansion retains a recursive reference when expanding it would keep growing the surrounding type. Specialization and materialization preserve the caller's mapping visitor, including active equivalence checks. Inference cycle recovery normalizes recursive applications' arguments without expanding their bound bodies.

The tests cover known-key precision, arbitrary keys, extra items, materialization, and operations on recursive values. They also check that invalid annotations and incompatible writes still produce diagnostics, and that valid union objects preserve the types they represent.

This migrates TypedDict value projections. Recursive intersections remain a limitation. Comparisons involving growing specializations are also conservative: a projection whose only concrete value type is `int` can still be rejected when assigned to `int` if its arguments keep growing.

Performance remains an open concern. The [ecosystem timing report](https://11e80cfe.ty-ecosystem-ext.pages.dev/timing) for revision `b2dcad6e69` records `scipy-stubs` at 1.79 seconds on the base and 2.35 seconds on the PR, a slowdown of about 32% in that CI run.

pulls.title: [ty] Share inference work for implicit type aliases
pulls.body:
## Summary

We reduce repeated work when checking implicit and PEP 613 type aliases, especially when a project builds unions from aliases imported across many files. For example:

```python
# aliases.py
Scalar = int | str
```

```python
# consumer.py
from aliases import Scalar

Value = Scalar | list[Scalar]

def consume(value: Value) -> None: ...
```

Checking this code involves two kinds of inference:

1. **Infer the assignments as values.** We resolve the names and infer the runtime values of the expressions. For example, `int` and `str` refer to class objects, and `int | str` produces a union object.
2. **Interpret the aliases as types.** When an alias is used in an annotation, we also interpret its right-hand side as a type expression and check for invalid alias cycles. Here, `int` and `str` denote instance types. This pass still needs some runtime information: checking that `|` is valid requires the runtime types of its operands.

Salsa already caches the completed inference queries, but these two computations do not share all their intermediate results. The second pass repeats name and attribute lookups and can infer the runtime operands of `|` again. Constructing unions and following imported aliases can also repeat work across inference regions.

This PR shares that work in three places:

- **Results from value inference.** We retain the resolved value type and source definition for each name or attribute, along with the lookup context. We also record which runtime expression types can be reused from the existing expression table; we do not store those types a second time. These saved results are persisted as `AliasInferenceInputs`: outputs of the value pass that serve as inputs to the type-expression pass. The later pass reuses them when the deferred-lookup and type-variable binding contexts match.
- **Union normalization.** We cache the simplified union for a given sequence of operand types and alias-expansion policy within a program. Previously, interning reused the final union's identity but did not avoid the work of constructing and simplifying it. Value inference and type-expression inference can use different expansion policies, so those results remain separate.
- **Imported-alias source resolution.** For the imported `Scalar`, we cache the lookup that follows imports and re-exports back to a unique source definition. We still examine all reachable definitions: two conditional definitions with the same runtime type do not establish a unique alias source.

Closes astral-sh/ty#4703.

pulls.title: Use a shared time budget for fuzzing
pulls.body:
Our `py-fuzzer` script currently limits each failing seed to have a maximum of 60 seconds for minimization, even when the CI job has time remaining. For example, in [this fuzz job on #29025](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/actions/runs/37632264340/job/112829497328), minimization timed out for seed 57 even though there would have been another 15 minutes before GitHub cancelled the CI job. Running the script locally demonstrated that pysource_minimize was [easily able](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29025#issuecomment-6064567417) to minimize the panic if only given slightly more time to do so.

This PR replaces the per-seed limit in CI with a global, shared budget for checking seeds and minimizing failures. Local runs have no overall budget by default. CI, however, records the job start time in its first step and passes it and the job timeout to the fuzzer, which subtracts elapsed setup and build time and reserves an additional 90 seconds for other job overhead and reporting. Individual calls to ty or Ruff still have a five-second timeout, allowing us to minimize hangs or pathological performance issues.

By default, the fuzzer reports failing seeds as they are found and prints completed minimizations. When the deadline is reached, it stops starting new seed and minimizer checks, reports the original source for unfinished minimizations, and identifies unchecked seeds. Checks already in progress can finish after the deadline. The logs and, when requested, the GitHub issue body include a command to rerun failing and unchecked seeds; the script exits with status 2 if any seeds were left unchecked.

Here are some mockups of what bot-opened issues could look like, using fictional data:

<details>
<summary>Issue with minimized, unminimized, and unchecked seeds</summary>

Run listed here: https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/actions/runs/1234567890

Each snippet caused ty to exit with a status other than 0, 1, or 2, or time out after five seconds during fuzzing.

Build ty from commit `0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567` with `cargo build --locked --bin=ty`. Save a snippet to `repro.py`, then run:

```
target/debug/ty check repro.py --python-version=3.10 --python-platform=linux
```


### Seed: 78

```python
class Example:
    pass
```

<details>
<summary>Seed: 93 (original source; minimization did not complete)</summary>

```python
class Original:
    value = [1, 2, 3]
    def method(self):
        return self.value
```

</details>

### Unchecked seeds

The time budget expired before 2 seeds could be checked.

- `123`
- `124`

To check all seeds that failed or were left unchecked, check out Ruff commit `0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567` and run from the repository root:

```shell
uv run --project=./python/py-fuzzer fuzz --bin=ty 78 93 123 124
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Issue with unchecked seeds and no failures</summary>

Run listed here: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/actions/runs/1234567890

Test executable: ruff at commit `0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567`.


### Unchecked seeds

The time budget expired before 3 seeds could be checked.

- `10`
- `11`
- `12`

To check all seeds that failed or were left unchecked, check out Ruff commit `0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567` and run from the repository root:

```shell
uv run --project=./python/py-fuzzer fuzz --bin=ruff 10 11 12
```

</details>

## Rejected alternatives

1. Keep a per-minimization budget, but just increase it (by a lot?).

   We could do this, and it fixes the theoretical problem that codex raised where a couple of seeds that take a very long time to minimize stop the script from even discovering bugs in later seeds (because it never even gets to those later seeds).

   I decided against this approach, however, because in practice I think it will only be hangs that take a _long_ time to minimize. We've seen in the past that a ty hang can cause the script as a whole to timeout in CI, but whenever it's done so in the past, it's never caused the script to fail to get onto non-hanging seeds. It's always been the case that the script has completed all seeds except the problematic ones that were causing it to hang. So I decided that per-minimization budgets were a solution looking for a problem.

2. Get rid of all budgets altogether, go back to something more similar to what the script was like prior to https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29045.

   This is very attractive, because it avoids a lot of the new complexity added in this PR to do with calculating budgets, interrupting subprocesses that have already been started, etc.
   
   I decided against this, however, because I do think the fact that the script now minimizes hangs substantially increases the risk that the script might finish without having finished minimizing all seeds. In the event that this happens, I _do_ think it's quite useful (though not essential) for the script to report which seeds it didn't get to, before GitHub cancels the CI job altogether.

pulls.title: [`ruff`] Allow suppressing unmatched-suppression-comment (RUF104)
pulls.body:
## Summary

This change allows `unmatched-suppression-comment` (`RUF104`) diagnostics to be suppressed using line-level (`# ruff: ignore[RUF104]`, `# noqa: RUF104`), file-level (`# ruff: file-ignore[RUF104]`, `# ruff: noqa: RUF104`), and block-level (`# ruff: disable[RUF104]`, self-suppression in `# ruff: disable[..., RUF104]`) directives without emitting spurious `RUF100` (`Unused suppression`) diagnostics.

### Root Cause
Previously, `check_suppressions` emitted `UnmatchedSuppressionComment` directly during its suppression pass without verifying whether `RUF104` was suppressed at the comment's location. Additionally, because this pass occurred after AST diagnostics had already been checked against suppressions, any comment intended to ignore `RUF104` was left marked as unused, triggering `RUF100`.

### Solution
1. Added `Suppressions::unmatched_disable_ranges` to identify candidate unmatched `disable` comments that were actually used.
2. Moved the generation of `RUF104` diagnostics into `check_noqa` immediately following AST diagnostic suppression resolution.
3. Routed `RUF104` through standard file exemption, range/ignore suppression, and line-level `noqa` directive matching.
4. When `RUF104` is suppressed, the suppressing directive/comment is marked as used, preventing subsequent `RUF100` warnings.
5. Removed direct `UnmatchedSuppressionComment` reporting from `Suppressions::check_suppressions`.

Closes #29106.

## Test Plan

- Added integration tests to `crates/ruff_linter/resources/mdtest/suppression/ignore.md` covering:
  - Trailing `ruff:ignore[RUF104]` on the same line as `# ruff:disable`
  - Preceding own-line `ruff:ignore[RUF104]`
  - Self-suppression via `# ruff:disable[T201, RUF104]`
  - Line-level `# noqa: RUF104`
  - File-level `# ruff:file-ignore[RUF104]`
  - Enclosing `# ruff:disable[RUF104]` block
  - Unused suppression verification for `RUF104`
- Verified test suite:
  ```bash
  cargo test -p ruff_mdtest --test mdtest -- suppression/ignore.md
  cargo test -p ruff_linter --lib -- rules::ruff::tests::range_suppressions
  cargo test -p ruff_linter --lib -- noqa
  cargo test -p ruff_linter --lib -- rules::ruff::tests
  cargo fmt --check
  cargo clippy -p ruff_linter --all-targets -- -D warnings
  ```

pulls.title: [ty] Avoid redundant inference for non-recursive union aliases
pulls.body:
## Summary

We now reuse inferred values for union aliases when we can prove that their source dependencies are acyclic, avoiding a second inference pass when aliases are chained or shared across modules.

A cached check follows unambiguous name and import references through unions and subscripts. Recursive aliases and cases the check cannot prove safe retain the existing type-expression inference and validation.

Refs astral-sh/ty#4703.

pulls.title: Use thin LTO for PGO training
pulls.body:
## Summary

We use thin LTO for the instrumented PGO training executable and keep fat LTO for the final release executable. This cuts estimated PGO pipeline time by **54%**, with essentially unchanged binary size.

| Measurement | Fat training | Thin training |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Instrumented build | 487.86 s | 85.50 s |
| Final fat-LTO build, median | 247.75 s | 250.43 s |
| Estimated complete PGO pipeline | 738.02 s | 338.26 s |
| Final stripped executable, median | 22.719 MiB | 22.724 MiB |

Linting and formatting on Django, pandas, scikit-learn, SciPy, and SymPy showed no consistent runtime regression across three independent profiles per mode. CPU changes ranged from -0.52% to +0.02%, and wall-time changes from -2.47% to +0.10% (positive means slower). Outputs matched across all six binaries. Individual profiles varied, and the pandas formatting results still allow a slowdown above 2%.

These are local Linux x86-64 measurements on an earlier revision; CI times and other platforms may differ.

pulls.title: [pylint] Avoid `PLW0108` false positive when callable is defined later
pulls.body:
## Summary

Fixes #24704.

Avoids reporting `PLW0108` (`unnecessary-lambda`) when the callable invoked inside the lambda (or any symbol it refers to) is defined later in an enclosing scope.

In Python, execution within a module, class, or function scope is sequential. When a callable is defined later in the file, referencing it eagerly at definition time produces a runtime `NameError` or `UnboundLocalError`:
```python
x = {"a": lambda y: f(y)}  # valid: f is resolved when called

def f(y):
    pass
```
If inlined to `x = {"a": f}`, evaluating `f` fails immediately with `NameError: name 'f' is not defined`.

This check verifies whether any referenced binding belongs to an enclosing ancestor scope and has a source start position after the lambda, suppressing the diagnostic and unsafe fix.

## Test Plan

- Added test fixtures in `crates/ruff_linter/resources/test/fixtures/pylint/unnecessary_lambda.py` covering module-level, class-level, function-level, and attribute targets.
- Updated snapshot tests via `INSTA_UPDATE=always cargo test -p ruff_linter unnecessary_lambda`.
- Verified all pylint tests pass: `cargo test -p ruff_linter pylint` (185 passed).
- Verified `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy -p ruff_linter -- -D warnings` exit cleanly.

pulls.title: fix(flake8-pyi): support stringized annotations in PYI036 (#27755)
pulls.body:
## Summary

Closes #27755.

`PYI036` (`bad-exit-annotation`) previously inspected raw annotation expressions directly, which caused false positive diagnostics for stringized (quoted) forms of otherwise-valid annotations (such as `tb: "TracebackType | None"`, `tb: "types.TracebackType | None"`, or `*args: "object"`). This also produced a conflict when autofixing `TC004` with `quote-annotations = true`.

This change leverages `Checker::match_maybe_stringized_annotation` to unwrap quoted annotations across all `PYI036` verification paths:
- Positional parameters in non-overloaded `__exit__` and `__aexit__` methods (both fully stringized unions and partially quoted inner elements, e.g. `typ: "type[BaseException]" | None`)
- Star-args (`*args: "object"`) in short parameter lists
- Positional parameters in overloaded `__exit__` and `__aexit__` methods

Invalid quoted annotations (e.g. `typ: "type[BaseException]"` without `| None` or `tb: "Exception | None"`) continue to be rejected with appropriate diagnostics.

## Test Plan

- Extended `crates/ruff_linter/resources/test/fixtures/flake8_pyi/PYI036.py` with test fixtures covering:
  - `GoodStringized`: quoted PEP 604 unions for `__exit__` and `__aexit__`
  - `GoodStringizedVariadic`: `*args: "object"`
  - `GoodStringizedOverload`: quoted parameter types in overloaded exit methods
  - `GoodStringizedObject`: quoted `"object"` annotations
  - `GoodPartiallyStringized`: quoted inner type with unquoted `| None`
  - `BadStringized`: invalid quoted annotations to verify diagnostics are still triggered
- Verified with `INSTA_UPDATE=no cargo test -p ruff_linter --lib rule_badexitannotation`
- Verified full rule suite: `cargo test -p ruff_linter --lib rules::flake8_pyi::` (130 passed)
- Verified formatting and lints: `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy -p ruff_linter --all-targets` (all clean)

pulls.title: [ty] Prevent unbounded nesting in cyclic decorator inference
pulls.body:
## Summary

Fixes a panic when a decorator returns a tuple containing the decorated definition and a later binding of that name supplies a concrete type. During inference, the concrete binding can displace the marker for the recursive reference. Each subsequent iteration then wraps the previous result in another tuple and never converges.

We restore the cycle marker when a new inference result embeds the complete previous result after the initial cycle iterations. Existing cycle normalization can then converge while retaining the outer tuple, so we still accept tuple assignments and reject incompatible ones. Matching complete results keeps unrelated type arguments and their correlations intact.

This recovery applies to value inference, including the inferred declarations of decorated functions and classes. Annotation scopes and raw type-alias and member queries keep their existing recovery: introducing value-cycle markers there would discard useful shape information in recursive annotated types.

pulls.title: [`pycodestyle`] Exclude `True`, `False`, and `None` from whitespace-around-keyword checks (`E271`-`E274`)
pulls.body:
## Summary

pycodestyle builds its keyword set for `E271`-`E274` as `keyword.kwlist + ['print'] - SINGLETONS`, so whitespace around `True`, `False`, and `None` is not checked. Ruff's `whitespace_around_keywords` gated on `token.kind().is_keyword()` alone, flagging pycodestyle-clean code like aligned dict values:

```python
values = {
    'X':    None,
    'XXXX': None,
}
```

`TokenKind` already has `is_singleton()` — the same predicate `E275` (`missing_whitespace_after_keyword`) uses — so the fix gates on `is_keyword() && !is_singleton()`. `E275` needed no change.

Note: an earlier PR for this (#29251) was closed by automation before review; the issue remains open. This reimplements the same approach with fixture coverage for the singleton cases.

## Test Plan

- Added `#: Okay` fixture cases to `E27.py` (aligned dict, assignment, call args with trailing spaces).
- `cargo test -p ruff_linter --lib -- pycodestyle::tests`: 148 passed; snapshot diffs show only the intended changes — diagnostics previously attributed to singletons (`True`-side `E271`/`E273`) now attribute to the real keyword on the other side where one exists (`and`-side `E272`), and disappear where none does.

### Rand is unsound with a custom logger using rand::rng()
[GHSA-cq8v-f236-94qc](https://redirect.github.com/advisories/GHSA-cq8v-f236-94qc)

<details>
<summary>More information</summary>

#### Details
It has been reported (by @​lopopolo) that the `rand` library is [unsound](https://rust-lang.github.io/unsafe-code-guidelines/glossary.html#soundness-of-code--of-a-library) (i.e. that safe code using the public API can cause Undefined Behaviour) when all the following conditions are met:

- The `log` and `thread_rng` features are enabled
- A [custom logger](https://docs.rs/log/latest/log/#implementing-a-logger) is defined
- The custom logger accesses `rand::rng()` (previously `rand::thread_rng()`) and calls any `TryRng` (previously `RngCore`) methods on `ThreadRng`
- The `ThreadRng` (attempts to) reseed while called from the custom logger (this happens every 64 kB of generated data)
- Trace-level logging is enabled or warn-level logging is enabled and the random source (the `getrandom` crate) is unable to provide a new seed

`TryRng` (previously `RngCore`) methods for `ThreadRng` use `unsafe` code to cast `*mut BlockRng<ReseedingCore>` to `&mut BlockRng<ReseedingCore>`. When all the above conditions are met this results in an aliased mutable reference, violating the Stacked Borrows rules. Miri is able to detect this violation in sample code. pulls.title: [ty] Check inferred defaults against inherited attribute read types
pulls.body:
## Summary

We now check the value of an unannotated attribute inherited from one base against the declared read type in another. Previously, we skipped the inferred attribute entirely, allowing incompatible values to replace a base's annotated type:

```python
class Declared:
    value: int = 0

class Number:
    value = 1

class Text:
    value = "text"

class Compatible(Number, Declared): ...  # OK
class Incompatible(Text, Declared): ...  # invalid-attribute-override
```

An inferred default still does not declare a restriction on later writes. In particular, the inferred `Literal[1]` in `Number` does not prevent writing another `int`. When a base itself has only an inferred default, it imposes no declared read or write type.

Part of https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/2158.

pulls.title: [ty] Return type inference
pulls.body: ## Summary This PR adds return type inference as a new feature to ty. The feature is currently *disabled by default*. Users can activate the feature by setting `analysis.return-type-inference` to `"always"`. In a standalone function, the inferred return type is simply the union of the types of all reachable `return`ed expressions, as shown in the image on the right. If control flow can reach the end of the function scope, we add `None` to the union. In a (non-final) method on a (non-final) class, we additionally union with `Unknown` to allow child classes to widen the intended return type. For example, imagine ```py class TaskBase: def compute(self): return None class IntTask(TaskBase): def compute(self): return 42 ``` Here, we infer a return type of `None | Unknown` for `TaskBase.compute`. Otherwise, if we inferred `None`, we would prohibit child classes from returning something else, which seems undesirable. Another interesting scenario is when the base class method is annotated, but the child class method is not: ```py class Base: def method(self) -> int: return 0 class Child(Base): def method(self): return 1 ``` Here, we respect the base class definition and infer `Child.method` as returning `int`, not `int | Unknown`. This work is based on https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/17371 by @mtshiba (thank you!) There are a few notable things that are _not_ implemented here: - The type of the function itself currently stays unchanged, that is: we do not infer a signature with the inferred return type. Concretely: `my_function()` may be inferred as `int`, but `my_function` itself would still be inferred as `def my_function() -> Unknown`. We have existing tests with TODOs for this and I plan to tackle this in a follow up. - We do not yet have return type inference for generator functions or async functions - We do not attempt to solve the problem of "escaping" inner types here (see tests with TODOs) - We do not add LSP/playground features related to this feature, but plan to do so soon (display return type hints). - There is a limitation around `functools.wraps` that's present in the ecosystem report. This will hopefully be solved by https://github.com/python/typeshed/pull/16515 - There is a [limitation around `NotImplemented`](https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/1150#issuecomment-6140701931) which hasn't been resolved yet. The solution is described [here](https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/1150#issuecomment-6147899750). - Fixpoint iteration currently uses `Divergent` as a provisional value. I did think about using the new μ-types, but that currently leaves too many questions unanswered: How would we represent an anonymous μ-type? How would the (provisional) recursive marker `R` interact with other types during inference (especially since those operations require "closed" recursive types, and `R` would still be open)? closes https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/128 ## Test Plan - Changed assertions in the previously reviewed & merged mdtests - Studied the ecosystem impact and addressed many problems

pulls.title: [ty] Accept regular attributes over nominal ClassVars
pulls.body:
## Summary

We now allow a regular class-body attribute to override a nominal base's `ClassVar`. The regular attribute permits every class operation the base allowed and also permits assignment through instances:

```python
from typing import ClassVar

class Base:
    value: ClassVar[int] = 0

class Regular(Base):
    value: int = 1  # Now accepted, with or without a default.
```

Incompatible read types still report `invalid-attribute-override`, and narrowing accepted writes still reports the opt-in `invalid-mutable-override`. Instance-only declarations and dataclass fields still cannot override a `ClassVar`. Explicit and structural protocol implementations still preserve their `ClassVar` qualifiers.

This is a nominal override policy choice. Mypy, Pyright and Pyrefly reject the regular-attribute example; the typing spec does not explicitly require that qualifier to persist through a nominal override. We favor the interpretation consistent with regular attributes supporting both class and instance operations.

Based on #28560. There is an overlapping proposal for the same issue in #27407.

Closes https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/3992.

pulls.title: [pycodestyle] Exclude None, True, and False from whitespace around keywords (E271, E272, E273, E274)
pulls.body:
﻿## Summary

Upstream pycodestyle explicitly excludes singleton literals (`False`, `None`, and `True`) from its `KEYWORDS` definition, but Ruff's `whitespace_around_keywords` only checked `token.kind().is_keyword()`. Consequently, aligned dictionary values and expressions involving singletons were erroneously reported under E271, E272, E273, and E274.

Excluding singleton tokens (`!token.kind().is_singleton()`) from keyword whitespace checks restores parity with pycodestyle.

Closes #29215.

## Test Plan

Added regression cases for dictionary alignment and singleton operands to `E27.py`, updated snapshot tests, and verified all linter tests pass via `cargo test -p ruff_linter` and `cargo clippy -p ruff_linter`.

x: type[X[str]] = X
reveal_type(x())  # revealed: X[str]

Resolves https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/1624.

pulls.title: [ty] Compute reaching definitions on demand
pulls.body:
## Summary

This adds a standalone query to the inference pipeline that returns the reaching definitions of a particular name. This is intended for eventual use in the language server for various features whose accuracy improves with reaching definitions (e.g., https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/1560 and https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/3410).

This is an alternative to #28423 that avoids retaining reaching definitions in cached type-inference results.

## Approach

[`ReachingDefinitions::for_name`](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/fa276d464a776bbb2867cf919e76d345496c1a70/crates/ty_python_semantic/src/semantic_model.rs#L68) runs type inference with a special instance of `TypeInferenceBuilder` whose [`infer_place_load`](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/fa276d464a776bbb2867cf919e76d345496c1a70/crates/ty_python_semantic/src/types/infer/builder.rs#L10722) method builds a [`DefinitionResolution`](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/fa276d464a776bbb2867cf919e76d345496c1a70/crates/ty_python_semantic/src/place/definitions.rs#L21) object that describes the definitions that reach that particular place load.

pulls.title: [ty] Avoid hangs in recursive aliases with invalid type arguments
pulls.body:
Checking mutually recursive implicit aliases can fail to converge when a generic helper carries a recursive reference in its type arguments:

```python
type Pair[T, U] = tuple[T, U]
A = tuple[int, "B"]
B = Pair[str, "A"]
```

Inspect stored alias arguments for recursive references before falling back to runtime-value inference, without evaluating alias bodies. The same issue occurs when an argument is invalid, such as replacing `str` above with a variable assigned `42`. That case also fails to converge with #29200, where implicit aliases containing invalid type forms still have a runtime-value fallback.

## Test Plan

mdtest updated

pulls.title: [ty] Use one member lookup engine for recursive proofs
pulls.body:
## Summary

Recursive type comparisons can return to the same obligation through member lookup, descriptor binding, callable upcasting, or inference. Every such operation must keep the proof that requested it: a completed result can be reused, but an incomplete lookup cannot count as a missing member or an established relationship.

Use one member lookup engine for ordinary lookup and for lookup within an active relation. The ordinary entry point starts a context; nested operations keep that context while selecting declarations, binding descriptors and checking their receiver. Getter and setter requirements, including protocol attributes, are resolved under the member obligation that needs them. Callable upcasting uses the same engine to inspect `__call__`.

Pure declaration queries remain cached separately from context-sensitive evaluation. Recursive aliases keep closed transformations, and comparisons of growing protocols reconstruct both original operands before using a universal proof. A failed generalization therefore cannot erase stored structure or leak constraints into the concrete comparison.

The tests cover recursive descriptor owners and growing callable members, including incompatible calls and finite nested specializations.

Depends on #29228. #29226 defers receiver obligations using the same operations.

pulls.title: [ty] Separate TypedDict value projection from normalization
pulls.body:
## Summary

Reading from a recursively specialized `TypedDict` can overflow the stack when constructing its value type starts another comparison that needs the same projection. For example, calling `get` here recursively compares the declared fields and extra items:

```python
from typing_extensions import ReadOnly, TypedDict

class A[T](TypedDict, extra_items=ReadOnly["B[B[T]]"]):
    child: "type[B[T]]"

class B[T](TypedDict, extra_items=ReadOnly["type[A[T]]"]):
    child: "A[T]"

def check(value: A[int]):
    value.get("child")
```

We now construct the union of declared field types and extra-item types without querying their relationships. Type comparisons use this structural projection, while ordinary observations normalize the completed union. This preserves canonical return types for dictionary methods without restarting comparisons during construction.

The regression tests cover legacy and PEP 695 generics, retain the precise type of known-key reads and all alternatives for arbitrary-key reads, and reject incompatible assignments. The full semantic suite passes at this head: 974 passed, with 34 skipped.

pulls.title: [ty] Skip impossible generic intersection comparisons
pulls.body:
Generic class-pattern narrowing can produce many intersections that share some class bounds while differing on others. Union normalization repeatedly creates cached relation queries to determine whether one alternative covers another.

Reject a comparison early when a generic target bound has no matching origin among the source bounds and all source classes have no explicit bases. Keep specialization and inheritance reasoning in the existing checker.

Related to astral-sh/ty#4676. Uses the generic benchmarks added in #29235. The successful-comparison shortcut proposed in #23799 is complementary.

## Test plan

Measured standard fat-LTO release builds of direct parent `c79af4610339` and head `702b13ca2bdc` on Apple Silicon macOS, with Python 3.12 fixtures. These builds do not use PGO. Criterion results use six matched head/parent process pairs with balanced run order and 10 samples per process; the 32-case CLI result uses four balanced pairs. Each phase excludes an initial warmup block. Process monitoring observed no competing compiler or checker activity during either measured phase.

Times are medians of process means for Criterion and of total process wall times for the CLI. Changes are geometric means of matched head/parent ratios, so they need not equal the ratio of displayed medians. Intervals are approximate paired bootstrap 95% intervals from these single-machine runs, without correction for multiple comparisons; the four-pair CLI interval is descriptive.

| Workload | Parent | Head | Paired time change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Generic 8 cases, Criterion | 73.8 ms | 57.1 ms | 22.6% faster (22.2–23.0%) |
| Generic 16 cases, Criterion | 1.215 s | 0.678 s | 44.3% faster (44.1–44.5%) |
| Generic 32 cases, CLI | 33.745 s | 14.496 s | 57.1% faster (56.6–57.7%) |
| Non-generic 8 cases, Criterion | 90.2 ms | 89.4 ms | No clear change: 0.3% faster (0.8% slower–1.4% faster) |
| Non-generic 16 cases, Criterion | 935.0 ms | 932.5 ms | No clear change: 0.6% faster (0.04% slower–1.2% faster) |

Every benchmark invocation used in the table completed without diagnostics. The Criterion and CLI phases each retain every planned sample and repetition.

The [CodSpeed comparison](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29240#issuecomment-6072183114) against the same direct parent reports four improvements and no regressions. CodSpeed flags differing runtime environments, which may affect its exact ratios; the same-machine release measurements above independently confirm the generic speedups.

pulls.title: [ty] Separate value and denoted expression maps
pulls.body:
## Summary

Type expressions denote types, while runtime consumers need the type of the evaluated value. For example, evaluating the argument of `TypeForm(Never)` produces an inhabited type-form object, even though the argument denotes `Never`.

Store value-expression types and denoted types in two disjoint maps of raw `Type` values. Value lookups wrap recorded type expressions in `TypeForm[T]`; annotation consumers read the denoted type directly. Merges and replacements keep each expression in exactly one map, and caches preserve both maps. IDE display retains the interpretation used during inference.

This is an alternative to #29238 for comparing memory use. Both implementations start from `88886a423ad1`. Two maps remove the enum tag from every retained entry, at the cost of an additional map header in each inference result. Scope maps deduplicate values separately in each map.

## Test plan

Used a standalone Rust layout probe against the debug build on aarch64 macOS. Key/value entries shrink from 48 bytes with the enum to 40 bytes with raw types. Two `FrozenMap` headers occupy 32 bytes instead of 16; two `FrozenValueMap` headers occupy 64 bytes instead of 32.

The layout measurement in #29238 with debug assertions disabled found 24-byte enum entries versus 20-byte raw-type entries. The memory reports on this PR and #29238 can compare the aggregate effect across projects.

pulls.title: [ty] Distinguish value and denoted expression types
pulls.body:
## Summary

Type expressions currently share storage with value expressions, even though their inferred types describe different things. For example, the argument in `TypeForm(Never)` denotes `Never`, but evaluating it produces an inhabited type-form object. Runtime analysis must not mistake that denoted type for the type of the evaluated value. The operand analysis in #28843 makes this distinction necessary.

Store expression types as `InferredExpressionType::Value(T)` or `InferredExpressionType::TypeExpression(T)`. Runtime consumers request the value interpretation, which wraps a recorded type expression in `TypeForm[T]`; annotation consumers request its denoted type. Carry the distinction through inference regions, expression caches, and cycle normalization. IDE display retains the interpretation used during inference.

## Test plan

Measured the Rust layouts on aarch64 macOS to assess the storage cost of the enum:

| Layout | `Type` → tagged value | Key/value entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Debug assertions disabled | 16 → 20 bytes | 20 → 24 bytes |
| Debug assertions enabled | 32 → 40 bytes | 40 → 48 bytes |

The `FrozenMap` and `FrozenValueMap` headers remain 16 and 32 bytes, respectively. Scope maps deduplicate tagged values, so their value-table cost depends on the number of distinct `(interpretation, type)` pairs. The memory report can establish the aggregate impact across projects.

pulls.title: [ty] Infer union parameters through call-wide constraints
pulls.body:
Union-parameter inference currently filters alternatives before combining evidence from all arguments. This can apply a type variable's bound to an argument that matches a different union member, or lose the relationship between type variables inferred from separate members.

Infer ordinary union parameters through the shared constraint relation so every argument member must match a parameter alternative and all arguments contribute to the same solution. Retain compatibility inference for variadics, recursive aliases, and gradual evidence.

Refs astral-sh/ty#3557 and astral-sh/ty#4277.

pulls.title: [ty] Preserve uncertain instance types in negative hasattr checks
pulls.body:
A failed `hasattr` check can currently narrow an instance with an annotated attribute to `Never`, even though the annotation does not initialize the attribute. Since ty does not enforce definite initialization, that can incorrectly make a missing-attribute branch unreachable.

Preserve uncertain instance types in negative `hasattr` branches, while continuing to exclude types whose ordinary class bindings or method contracts establish presence. For example, a missing `value` remains possible for `Annotated` but excludes `WithDefault`:

```python
class Annotated:
    value: int

class WithDefault:
    value: int = 1

def f(obj: Annotated | WithDefault) -> None:
    if not hasattr(obj, "value"):
        reveal_type(obj)  # Annotated
```

The presence check examines actual class-body bindings across the MRO and recognizes methods declared in protocols and stubs. Instance assignments, annotation-only declarations, slots, properties, uncertain descriptors, conditional bindings, and transformed dataclass-like/Pydantic fields do not establish presence on instances.

Negative narrowing also preserves known module and class-object attributes. Modules use unconditional source bindings or explicit stub declarations. Class objects use class bindings and ordinary metaclass bindings; built-in property objects and slot descriptors establish presence on the defining class even when the corresponding instance attribute can be absent. Dynamic attribute fallbacks and potentially failing descriptor access remain uncertain.

Negative checks filter the currently known alternatives without retaining a negated structural protocol. This prevents a later intersection with an annotated instance type from incorrectly making that type impossible. Within a conjunction, the presence filters run after the other narrowing constraints. Positive `hasattr` narrowing and its `bool` return type are unchanged.

Related: [ty#2455](https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/2455).

B008 was flagging frozen dataclasses when they were used as default values in arguments. Since these classes are immutable, this wasn't needed. It would flag code such as `def f(x: Foo = Foo())` when `Foo` is a dataclass with `frozen=True`.

## Solution

pulls.title: [ty] Represent protocol applications as recursive type constructors
pulls.body:
## Summary

We check recursive protocol methods whose return types contain nested intersections and exclusions without overflowing the stack. Repeated calls preserve specialized protocol arguments, including inherited members such as those in [ty#4694](https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4694).

A protocol application uses `RecursiveType` to store its declaration, type arguments, and deferred operations. Substitution transforms the application without expanding member signatures. Type comparisons unfold the structural interface when needed; member lookup and metadata queries retain the protocol's declaration and nominal identity.

Specialization and materialization retain their order when we observe members, including descriptors and the opposite read and write polarities of mutable attributes. Materializing a protocol containing a type variable and subsequently replacing that variable with `Any` agrees with the corresponding scalar, tuple, and list behavior. Explicit `Top[P[Any]]` and `Bottom[P[Any]]` remain distinct.

Depends on #29227. Related to #29218.

Closes https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4099.
Closes https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4691.

pulls.title: [ty] Add structural substitution for recursive protocol construction
pulls.body:
## Summary

Constructing a recursive protocol member can ask whether its own components are subtypes before those components exist. Substitution into a union or intersection can then recursively request the member it is still building.

Extend the structural union builder from #29241 to intersections and type mappings. An explicitly structural substitution flattens unions and restores disjunctive normal form without starting subtype or disjointness queries. It preserves aliases and recursive declarations and maps their stored arguments. Ordinary substitutions keep semantic normalization by default.

A separate normalization mapping simplifies a completed callable when its signature is exposed. This change supplies the construction primitives; protocol member lookup and receiver binding keep their existing behavior.

Depends on #29241.

pulls.title: [ty] Defer receiver constraints until callable use
pulls.body:
## Summary

Binding an explicitly annotated receiver can start type comparisons while its recursive callable is still being constructed. Keep the receiver obligation in the signature until comparison, invocation, or conversion to a regular callable can check it. Chained calls retain their inferred results while incompatible receivers and assignments are rejected.

Receiver inference preserves exact bindings shared by every viable path and leaves bounds that explicit arguments can widen available for later inference. Calls and descriptor binding check those obligations in the active relation and use the shared member lookup engine.

Depends on #29243.

pulls.title: [ty] Make microbenchmarks easier to read
pulls.body:
## Summary

The ty microbenchmarks often repeat Criterion setup and construct Python samples using escaped newlines, making the samples harder to read and edit. This refactors the benchmark definitions:

- Move the common setup into `benchmark_micro_case`. It preserves the existing execution model: initialize Rayon, prepare a fresh case for each `iter_batched_ref` input using `BatchSize::SmallInput`, and assert that `db.check()` produces no diagnostics. Benchmarks expecting other diagnostic counts keep their separate setup and assertions.
- Replace most `\n` escapes in the Rust strings with actual line breaks. Indent the Python alongside the surrounding Rust: `setup_micro_case` already removes common indentation before writing the source, leaving the relative indentation of Python blocks intact.
- Replace many raw Rust strings with ordinary strings containing single-quoted Python literals. The single- and double-quoted forms represent the same values in these samples, and the Python quotes no longer need escaping inside Rust strings.
- Simplify some source generation. For example, build `C0 | C1 | ...` with an iterator join instead of a manual separator loop, preserving the class order. The numbers of generated classes, match arms, and repeated statements remain the same.

Some generated samples gain blank lines, and others use different quote characters. These changes preserve the Python statements and literal values, but alter the source text and locations.

pulls.title: [ty] Preserve recursive protocol specializations across subtype proofs
pulls.body:
We avoid stack overflows and cyclic-query failures when specializing and comparing recursive protocol methods, including methods with generic receiver annotations and `Self` return types:

```python
from typing import Any, Protocol

class A[T](Protocol):
    value: T
    def f[U](self: A[U]) -> A[U & ~A[U & Any]]: ...

def chain[T](x: A[T]):
    return x.f().f()
```

We specialize protocol members when their types are needed and carry recursive signature obligations through the resulting type operations. Declared method classification reads metadata without expanding signatures, and recursive-member detection includes inherited protocol bases. Recursion filtering follows declared `Self` bounds without substituting a receiver that could trigger another protocol comparison. Intersection simplification retains an exclusion when removing it would require a circular proof. Pruning a constrained type variable's choices uses the same non-circular proof.

Callable comparisons retain the receiver type and its annotation until their compatibility can be checked under the signature recursion guard. Substitution therefore transforms those types without solving receiver constraints. Method preparation is guarded before binding `Self`, including when the implementation is a type variable bounded by a protocol. These guards also use the complete set of declaration identities retained by transparent decorators on overloaded callables. Callable unions retain their intrinsic descriptor provenance so their preparation can use the same guard without treating custom descriptor overload selection as fixed.

Constraint projection retains the same recursion state when it derives additional type relations. Results that depend on the active proof stay local to that proof. Union simplification during projection and descriptor binding also shares this context and retains terms when removing them would require a circular proof. Custom descriptor calls preserve that context through type-argument inference and use an uncached lookup while a proof is active. If normalization revisits an unfinished member comparison, we retain the union alternatives; the ordinary compatibility check still checks the descriptor's selected requirements. Nested mappings, including `Self` binding on descriptor read types, preserve the existing recursion context while keeping their substitution caches separate.

Receiver inference still specializes variables when all complete constraint paths agree on an exact type, and respects their declared bounds and constraints. Materialization distinguishes receivers already captured by bound methods from receivers required by protocol members. Its no-op proof checks type-argument prerequisites before expanding protocol interfaces. Metaclass `__call__` methods use the existing constructor override policy: signatures may differ unless marked `@override`.

The regressions cover repeated calls, inherited recursive members, receiver inference and rejection, overload selection, and materialization in both generic syntaxes. This also prevents the inherited-protocol regression reported in https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4694.

Closes https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4099.
Closes https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4691.

pulls.title: Treat more `collections` and `weakref` containers as mutable
pulls.body:
## Summary

Closes #25173

This PR changes behavior of flake8-bugbear in regard to `weakref.WeakKeyDictionary`, `weakref.WeakValueDictionary`, `weakref.WeakSet`, `collections.ChainMap`, `collections.UserDict`, `collections.UserList`, and `collections.UserString`, so that instead of reporting the error B008 ("function call in argument defaults"), it reports B006 ("mutable data structures for argument defaults"). These types are similar to `dict` and `list` in terms of being containers and are considered to be mutable, and therefore are suitable for B006, allowing for fixing the code via replacing a default value with `None` and making the object construction inside the body of the function.

### Implementation details

In this PR, those seven types are added to `is_mutable_return_type` in `crates/ruff_python_stdlib/src/typing.rs` file along with other types like `dict`, `list`, `set`, `Counter`, `OrderedDict`, `defaultdict`, and `deque`. As B008 purposefully skips objects matching `is_mutable_return_type` condition, this solves the categorization mistake while avoiding duplicates.

As discussed with maintainers, this change doesn't use `--preview` option. Because `is_mutable_return_type` is a shared helper, another side effect of this PR is that B039, RUF008, RUF012, RUF024, and PLW2901 rules will also treat those seven types as mutable data structures. According to the review comments, `collections.UserList` and `collections.UserString` are also included; even though `str` is immutable, a `UserString` instance is mutable due to `.data` attribute being reassignable.

## Test Plan

A new mdtest was added at `crates/ruff_linter/resources/mdtest/flake8-bugbear/mutable-argument-default.md`.

The new mdtest is set up to generate results for B006 and B008 and to include a single import case per type. The purpose of the test is to verify that B006 is triggered and that B008 ignores all those seven types strictly.

No `ruff_linter` snapshot changes in the existing tests. Ecosystem check results come from CI.

pulls.title: Use one codegen unit for release builds
pulls.body:
## Summary

We use one codegen unit for release builds and keep the profiling profile at 16. The measurements show lower peak memory and some runtime improvements, but slower PGO builds, including a large Windows regression.

- **Binary size:** Linux x86_64 shrank from 22.78 to 22.57 MiB (0.9%); macOS ARM64 shrank from 20.82 to 19.42 MiB (6.7%). Windows x86_64 grew from 25.128 to 25.158 MiB (0.12%).
- **Build time:** Combined instrumented and profile-use compilation increased from 6m 36s to 8m 16s on Linux (25%), from 5m 21s to 5m 57s on macOS (11%), and from 8m 18s to 57m 37s on Windows (6.9×). Instrumented builds were faster on all three platforms, but final profile-use builds were slower. The Windows profile-use build increased from 3m 04s to 52m 53s, with sustained compiler CPU use.
- **Memory:** Sampled peak process RSS across both build stages fell from 4.57 to 3.22 GiB on Linux (29%), from 9.86 to 7.20 GiB on macOS (27%), and from 4.17 to 3.15 GiB on Windows (25%).
- **Runtime performance:** Diagnostics and formatting-check output matched across 16 workloads. Both binaries produced identical formatted contents for 1,374 files, including the same 933 changed files. Across two rounds of 30 paired trials, held-out CPython linting was 6.8–7.0% faster on Linux and 3.3–3.7% faster on macOS. On Windows, single-thread CPython linting was 4.3–4.5% faster, and CPython formatting checks were 2.4–3.0% faster. No measured workload showed a consistent slowdown across both rounds. The timed suite covers default-rule linting, formatting checks, populated caches, and startup; formatter writes were checked for correctness outside timing.

The [comparison](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/actions/runs/37715474659) uses Rust 1.99.0, fat LTO, and the production PGO training corpus on the same source revision. Build times are single-run observations from clean target directories, in 16-then-1 order on each runner; OS cache and order effects remain possible. Memory peaks are sampled every 0.5 seconds. Linux uses the native GNU build environment rather than the manylinux packaging container. Other release targets were not measured.

pulls.title: Fail the manifest-digest step when the digest cannot be read
pulls.body:
## The step that exports the manifest digest cannot fail

In `build-docker.yml`, `docker-publish` and `docker-republish` each contain:

```bash
digest="$(
  docker buildx imagetools inspect "${IMAGE}:${VERSION}" --format '{{json .Manifest}}' \
  | jq -r '.digest'
)"
echo "digest=${digest}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
```

GitHub's default shell is `bash -e {0}`, which has **no pipefail**, so the command
substitution takes jq's exit status rather than the pipeline's. `inspect` can fail and the
step still succeeds.

Two failure modes, both run rather than reasoned about:

| input | current result | exit |
|---|---|---|
| `inspect` fails | `digest=""` | 0 |
| JSON parses but has no `.digest` | `digest="null"` | 0 |

Either value is written to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT` and passed to `actions/attest` as
`subject-digest`, so if anything surfaces it does so one step later and describes the wrong
thing.

## The change

`set -euo pipefail` plus `jq -e`, applied to both copies:

```
inspect fails        -> exit 4
null .digest         -> exit 1
happy path           -> exit 0, digest unchanged
```

Four lines, no behaviour change on the success path, and the failure now lands on the step
that actually failed.

## How this was found

A linter I maintain for CI checks that cannot fail flagged it. Worth saying plainly that the
same tool reported 21 HIGH findings against this repository and **18 were false**: it did not
understand that `required-checks-passed` reads every upstream through
`env: NEEDS_JSON: ${{ toJSON(needs) }}`, which is a perfectly good gate. Those were bugs in my
tool, fixed, and are not being reported here. These three survived manual review, and the two
blocks above are the same block twice.

I have not run the Docker publish workflows, since they need registry credentials and a
release tag. The claim here is about shell exit-status semantics, and the table above is
reproducible with `jq` alone.

pulls.title: [ty] Check writable __class__ before treating protocols as universal
pulls.body:
Protocols declaring a writable `__class__: type[object]` incorrectly accept arbitrary objects, and `type[P]` accepts classes whose instances fail that write requirement. The universal-protocol check tests `object` itself and treats the protocol as equivalent to `object`, even though each subclass's inherited setter accepts only `type[Self]`.

Check the required write against an arbitrary receiver type before taking the universal-protocol shortcut. Read-only `__class__` protocols and writable contracts accepting only `type[Self]` or `Never` retain their existing behavior.

This fixes the pre-existing structural-protocol bug exposed by #29200.

## Test plan

Manually compared a reduced scipy-stubs overload example before and after the fix. With an earlier object-array overload accepting `type[JustObject]` and a later floating-array overload accepting `type[Floating]`, passing `Floating` previously inferred `ObjectArray`; it now infers `FloatingArray`.

## Ecosystem report

At head [`588c1f8392`](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/commit/588c1f8392da077263686f10d41f89c1e5901cf2), all 21 stable scipy-stubs changes are expected: corrected overload selection removes 12 type assertion failures and 7 incorrect deprecation warnings, and adds 2 correct deprecation warnings. No ecosystem regressions found. [Full analysis](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29207#issuecomment-6048924278).

pulls.title: [ty] Preserve distinct string literal displays without deprecated ICU data
pulls.body:
Canonical equivalence can make distinct string values look the same. ty escapes their displays to distinguish them, but the current approach relies on ICU4X's deprecated `NfcInert` property, which [ICU4X plans to remove](https://github.com/unicode-org/icu4x/issues/7892), and can escape characters that do not need escaping.

Replace inertness checks with NFC checks on runs of unescaped text. When adding a character would make a run non-NFC, escape that character and continue checking after it. The resulting string literal is in NFC and evaluates to the original value, so canonically equivalent values remain distinguishable.

For example, `\u212b` (the Angstrom sign) is canonically equivalent to `Å`. ty now keeps the unrelated `é` visible while still distinguishing the two values:

```py
reveal_type("éÅ")
# main:    Literal["éÅ"]
# this PR: Literal["éÅ"]

reveal_type("é\u212b")
# main:    Literal["\xe9\u212b"]
# this PR: Literal["é\u212b"]
```

The change also uses Unicode grapheme-break properties to keep characters visually separate from the quotes and escape sequences around them. It escapes the braille blank because it can look like an ordinary space.

pulls.title: [ty] Retry inference for unsatisfiable return-context preferences
pulls.body:
Nested generic calls can reject valid arguments when a return-context preference passes the initial compatibility checks but makes the combined argument constraints unsatisfiable. For example, this reports an argument error expecting `list[object]`, although inferring `T = str` makes the calls and return valid:

```python
def wrap[T](x: list[T]) -> list[T]:
    return x

def identity[T](x: T) -> T:
    return x

def outer(x: list[str]) -> list[object] | list[str]:
    return identity(wrap(x))
```

Retry inference without the return-context preference when the preferred solve is proven unsatisfiable. If the retry is also unsatisfiable, retain the original diagnostic mapping: replacing it with recovery types containing `Unknown` can hide argument errors. Otherwise, use the retry's inference and diagnostics, preserving correlated alternatives and completeness information. Incomplete and budget-exhausted preferred solves do not trigger a retry.

Constructor calls are excluded: their inference stages share a specialization, and retrying just one stage can produce inconsistent type arguments. Context-sensitive arguments that have already been inferred too broadly, such as nested collection literals, remain a separate limitation.

This will go away with the broader contextual-inference refactor in #26680, but in the meantime it is a fairly narrow fix that improves inference and diagnostics, and avoids new false-positive ecosystem regressions in #29014.


## Ecosystem report

Analyzed head [`8ff68ffc05`](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/commit/8ff68ffc05bcf9dd5d1e4e9ce19339ce493388c7): 13 expected diagnostic removals in Meson and pandas. Nested token factories and regex compilation now infer the valid string specialization. No regressions were identified; CI passed and the PR is ready for review. [Full ecosystem report](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29205#issuecomment-6049215695).

pulls.title: [ty] Skip impossible nominal-complement union proofs
pulls.body:
Union normalization can attempt an expensive proof that two types together cover `object`. Skip that proof when both operands have a non-`object` nominal bound: neither can contain an instance of the bare `object` class, so their union cannot cover it. This also applies to positive intersection components and nominal types with gradual arguments or bases.

Related to astral-sh/ty#4676.

pulls.title: [ty] Avoid recursion guards for non-generic nominal targets
pulls.body:
Comparisons between nominal instances with a non-generic target only inspect MRO class identities. Skip the recursion guard for these comparisons, avoiding its bookkeeping. Tuple targets and specialized generic targets retain the guard because their element or type-argument comparisons can recurse.

Related to astral-sh/ty#4676.

## Test plan

Parent: `4830211afdd4`. Head: `10168bb1e5dc`.

Measured on Apple Silicon with macOS 26.7.1 using optimized debug builds (opt-level 1, LTO off). Criterion values are medians of three run means; CLI values are medians of 15 warmed runs, with variants interleaved. Reductions use geometric means of matched head/parent ratios (which differ from ratios of the displayed medians); small Criterion differences remain uncertain with only three rounds.

| Workload | Parent median | Head median | Paired time reduction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 8 cases, Criterion | 0.195 s | 0.175 s | +9.1% |
| 16 cases, Criterion | 1.874 s | 1.687 s | +11.6% |

pulls.title: [ty] Simplify string literal display escaping
pulls.body:
`icu_properties` 2.3 deprecates `NfcInert`, which ty uses to distinguish canonically equivalent strings in literal type displays. Upgrade `icu_properties` and simplify the display logic by dropping the NFC-based escaping that relies on that property.

ty no longer adds escapes solely to make canonically equivalent strings look different. For example:

```py
reveal_type("é")
# main:    Literal["é"]
# this PR: Literal["é"]

reveal_type("e\u0301")
# main:    Literal["e\u0301"]
# this PR: Literal["é"]
```

These strings remain distinct, but their displayed types can now look identical. ty still escapes default-ignorable characters and combining marks that would otherwise attach to a quote or an escape sequence; its output remains valid Python.

The alternative in #29193 uses a conservative heuristic to retain the distinction. This approach gives it up to avoid needing a replacement for `NfcInert`.

pulls.title: [ty] Infer implicit aliases from their definitions
pulls.body:
Implicit aliases currently fall back to their runtime values whenever independent type inference produces a nonrecursive type. Infer eligible aliases from their defining expressions in both recursive and nonrecursive cases, preserving generic parameters through forwarding and imports.

This lets `Alias = int | "str"` retain `int | str` in annotations while still reporting its runtime operator error. Ordinary values remain invalid as annotations, and aliases of classes, type variables, and special forms retain their constructor and identity rules. Definition lookup stays behind a tracked query so unrelated edits in an imported module do not invalidate consumers.

Prepares https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4683. Runtime `|` behavior is unchanged.

pulls.title: [ty] Preserve tuple shape when pattern expansion exceeds its budget
pulls.body:
After tuple pattern expansion reaches its budget, later cases can repeatedly analyze the large union of tuple alternatives left by earlier cases. Coalesce those alternatives while preserving tuple length and the union of types at each position. This bounds the remaining tuple representation and keeps useful capture types, while giving up correlations between positions. Carry the exhausted state through later cases so coalescing cannot repeatedly restart expansion.

Increase the alternative budget from 64 to 128; the existing 4,096-element budget still applies. Expansion remains exact until either budget is exhausted.

Fixes astral-sh/ty#4676.

pulls.title: [ty] Replace the deprecated NFC-inert property with a conservative heuristic
pulls.body:
`icu_properties` 2.3 deprecates `NfcInert`. This PR updates `icu_properties` and explores a replacement for the property as an alternative to #29166.

When displaying string literal types, ty escapes characters in non-NFC portions of a string so that canonically equivalent strings, such as `Å` and `Å`, can be distinguished. NFC-inert characters are unchanged by NFC and do not interact with adjacent characters during normalization; they can act as boundaries between the portions ty checks. The replacement recognizes only a conservative subset of these characters, so ty may unnecessarily escape other inert characters and characters in the same portion.

For example:

```py
reveal_type("é⏱\u212b")
# main:    Literal["é⏱\u212b"]
# this PR: Literal["\xe9\u23f1\u212b"]
```

The stopwatch character is NFC-inert, but the heuristic doesn't recognize it. As a result, ty checks the whole input as one portion and escapes `é` and `⏱` as well as `\u212b`, making the displayed type less readable.

Would this trade-off be acceptable, or should we instead ask ICU4X for a supported API for normalization boundaries or inertness?

pulls.title: [ty] Specialize inherited dataclass field converters
pulls.body:
Concrete subclasses of generic dataclass-transform classes retained the base class's type variables in inherited converter inputs, rejecting valid constructor calls, attribute assignments, and `__replace__` calls. Specialize the types stored in field metadata so these operations accept the subclass's concrete type arguments.

Apply type mappings to field defaults and converter input/output types, and avoid applying the specialization twice when collecting Pydantic right-hand-side defaults.

Fixes astral-sh/ty#4677.

## Test plan

Manually compared constructor signatures for equivalent right-hand-side and `Annotated` Pydantic field defaults using minimal local stubs before and after the change. Both forms retained matching defaults under generic specialization.

pulls.title: [ty] Give Self type variables distinct class identities
pulls.body:
Currently, all `Self` type variables share a single `TypeVarIdentity`. This isn't really semantically right, but it's mostly fine in practice, because they get bound to different methods and so have distinct `BoundTypeVarIdentity`. It does cause bugs in some cases with synthesized methods: unions of `_replace` methods from different named tuple classes can collapse to a single callable because their synthetic `Self` variables share an identity. This can incorrectly accept a callable promised to return only one of the classes, depending on the union order.

Also, we currently have to recover the owning class of a `Self` type variable via its upper bound (which should be set to the owning class), but this is a bit implicit and can be awkward when we transform upper bounds (e.g. for `type[T]` or due to specialization or materialization).

Instead, give class-owned `Self` variables explicitly distinct identities using `SelfTypeVarOrigin::Class`. Keep that origin stable when specializing or materializing their bounds, and represent receiver placeholders and synthesized `TypedDict` schemas with explicit unit variants.

pulls.title: Exclude file-watcher tests from sandbox testing guidance
pulls.body:
## Summary

Some sandboxed environments do not deliver file-watcher events, causing ty's `file_watching` integration tests to time out when codex tries to run the full suite of tests in our workspace. We already have guidance that tells codex that this is likely to happen, but codex usually tries to run them first anyway because we give it exact commands to run when trying to run tests. This PR therefore updates the exact recommended commands so that it doesn't even try to run the file-watching tests unless it's specifically working on a file-watching PR.

The `cargo test` fallback selects ty's remaining test targets explicitly because `cargo test` does not provide a binary-exclusion option.

pulls.title: [`pylint`] Detect reversed and inverted comparisons in `boolean-chained-comparison` (`PLR1716`)
pulls.body:
## Summary

Closes #29169.

At the moment, PLR1716 catches comparisons only if the two comparisons are already in the order of chain. It fails to detect logical condition identity in the following cases:

- Comparisons are swapped: `b < c and a < b`
- Operator in one of the comparisons is flipped: `b > a and b < c`, `b < c and b > a`, `a < b and c > b`
- Comparisons are swapped and both comparisons use `>`: `b > c and a > b`

### What this PR does

- This PR rewrites each comparison in one direction internally (for `x > y` uses `y < x`). When the two comparisons contain the same variable name in the middle, the comparison form a chain.
- Formats the result of suggestion using `>` (`a > b > c`) only when the operators in both comparisons are `>` or `>=`. Otherwise, the suggestion uses `<` (`a < b < c`).
- Respects the parentheses on the outer operand in order to avoid errors in expressions like `b < c and (x or y) < b`.
- Leaves the case with comparisons in order untouched (the current fix stays as safe).

### Preview

As PLR1716 has been a stable rule since Ruff 0.9.0 release, the new detection will work only in preview mode. This is done by adding `is_boolean_chained_comparison_reversed_enabled` helper to `preview.rs` file.

### Fix safety

The fixes of the new inverted/reversed case are considered as unsafe for the following reasons:

- **Short-circuiting and Evaluation Order:** Ordering changes evaluation order of operands and some of them could be even skipped because of short-circuiting.
- **Dunder methods:** Flipping `b > a` to `a < b` causes calling `__lt__` instead of `__gt__`. For custom classes it could be different behavior for the method.

The rule documentation is extended by "Fix safety" section and note about preview usage.

## Test Plan

- New fixture tests are added for swapped order of comparisons, flipped operator case, swapped chain with `>`, comparisons and operands surrounded by parentheses (`(x or y)`, `(a < d)`, `(not x)`, `(x if y else z)`).
- New preview snapshot test (`preview_rules` in `pylint/mod.rs`) is added, which provides 20 new diagnostics without any removed.
- The stable snapshot test is verified, providing no additional diagnostics (extra context lines are added).

Local checks pass:

```bash
cargo test -p ruff_linter rules::pylint # (186 passed)
cargo clippy -p ruff_linter --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --check
```

pulls.title: [ty] Separate nested symbol access from keyword-unpacking analysis
pulls.body:
## Summary

Preserving local dictionaries during keyword unpacking currently requires semantic indexing to classify every symbol use as keyword unpacking or something else. That call-specific rule also reaches into capture resolution and write tracking.

We now record whether a nested scope may read or write a name as a general symbol fact. The call layer uses the existing expression-scope and use-def indexes to identify other uses, caching the result once per qualifying function. This removes `SymbolUse` and restores the ordinary meaning of `mark_used`. It preserves the existing restrictions on annotated, aliased, mutated, captured, or ambiguously assigned dictionaries.

Core, semantic, and IDE tests pass: 2,941 tests before and after. In eight interleaved measurements per workload with optimized development binaries and one worker thread, Ruff's scripts were effectively unchanged (267 ms vs. 267 ms median). A stress case with 25 levels of nested functions increased from 253 ms to 257 ms. The other cases ranged from -4.7% to -0.3%, with overlapping timing ranges; all six workloads produced identical diagnostics.

pulls.title: [ty] Show documentation for annotation operators on hover
pulls.body:
Hovering over `~`, `&`, or `|` in an annotation now shows the documentation for `ty_extensions.Not`, `ty_extensions.Intersection`, or `typing.Union`, respectively. This also works in quoted annotations and explicit type aliases. The annotation check is syntactic. It recognizes function and variable annotations, explicit type aliases, and PEP 695 type parameter bounds, constraints, and defaults. It can therefore treat operators in `Annotated` metadata or `Literal` arguments as type operators. For example, hovering over `~` in `Annotated[int, ~flags]` can show the documentation for `Not`. It does not yet recognize type expressions in `cast()` or functional `TypeVar`, `NamedTuple`, and `TypedDict` declarations. We can improve on all these shortcomings in followups if we feel it's important; for now, I think this is certainly good enough for an MVP, however. The `ty_extensions` docstrings are also updated to describe the operator spellings. Closes https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4037. ## Screenshots using a local playground build

pulls.title: [`flake8-type-checking`] Never flag annotations in function scopes
pulls.body:
Fixes #29182

## Summary

`flake8-type-checking.runtime-evaluated-decorators` erroneously applied runtime semantics to all annotation assignments inside a function scope. Annotation assignments inside function scopes never result in any actual code for the annotation expressions, they get silently dropped by the compiler and are missing completely from the resulting byte code, so they can never be anything other than typing-only.

## Test Plan

`cargo nextest run`

pulls.title: [parser] implement optional depth limits
pulls.body:
## Summary

Add back depth limits while parsing that were removed by #25464.

#25464 used stacker to avoid stack overflow while parsing deeply nested code, however that introduces a new risk - unlimited memory use. The memory growth can't even be caught by our custom allocator in monty since it uses `mmap`.

We tried to work around this in Monty with https://github.com/pydantic/monty/pull/906, but it's brittle and introduces a performance penalty by parsing the source twice (3 times if you included type checking).

This could also be implemented as a crates feature to avoid any runtime impact by default, but that seemed unnecessary given there's no noticable performance impact to this change.

## Test Plan

This work includes tests.

pulls.title: [`pylint`] Preserve trailing comments in `useless-return` fix (`PLR1711`)
pulls.body:
## Summary

Closes #28861

The `useless-return` rule (PLR1711) removes the final `return` / `return None`
in a function. When that line had a trailing comment, the fix deleted the whole
line and the comment was lost — and the fix was still marked safe.

This keeps a trailing comment on its own line instead of deleting it, the same
way `PIE790` and `PYI013` already do. If removing the statement would still drop
a comment (for example a comment inside a parenthesized multi-line return), the
fix is now marked unsafe rather than silently deleting it. I also added a "Fix
safety" section to the rule docs.

One thing I wasn't sure about: pragma-style trailing comments like `# noqa` or
`# fmt: off` can change meaning when moved onto their own line. I left them as
ordinary comments for now (matching PIE790/PYI013), but happy to special-case
them if you'd prefer.

## Test Plan

Added fixture cases to `useless_return.py`: the example from the issue, a method
with `return None  # ...`, a `return;` with a comment, a same-line
`print(...); return  # ...`, and a multi-line parenthesized return (the unsafe
case). The existing `# [useless-return]` comments now survive in the snapshot.
`cargo test -p ruff_linter`, clippy, and the formatting hooks all pass.
